Refrigerators and cold stores at a temperature of 1 to 4° C stop the proliferation of pathogenic bacteria but not of food spoilage bacteria. Campylobacter is also referred to as a foodborne disease because it remains dormant at room temperature but multiplies rapidly at body temperature (37 °C); it is destroyed at temperatures above 48 C. Most cases of salmonella food poisoning are caused by storing prepared food at room temperature. Salmonella is quickly destroyed at temperatures above 74 degrees Celsius Other food-borne pathogens include Listeria, E. coli and Clostridium perfringens, which forms spores and can survive cooking. Both Campylobacter and Salmonella are associated with raw meat, poultry, eggs, and unpasteurized milk. Examples of cross-contamination include kitchen staff failing to wash their hands when removing eggs from the fridge, a drop of juice from fresh chicken at the top of the fridge contaminating cooked food down, and using the same cutting board to prepare meat and vegetables. Infestation is not usually from person to person.

premise: Time to cool it Refrigerators are the embodiment of clunky technology: solid, reliable and just a little boring. They haven't changed much over the past century, but then they shouldn't have. They're based on a powerful, efficient idea - draw heat from the thing you want to cool by evaporating liquid next to it, then dump that heat by pumping the steam elsewhere and condensing it. This method of pumping heat from place to place served humanity well when the main functions of refrigerators were food preservation and, as air conditioners, cooling buildings. Today's high-tech world, however, requires high-tech refrigeration. Heat pumps are no longer in service. The search for something to replace them. ONE GROUP OF CANDIDATES IS KNOWN AS PARAELECTRIC MATERIALS. These behave like batteries when they undergo a temperature change: electrodes are attached to them and they generate current. This effect is used in infrared cameras. AN ARRAY OF TINY PIECES OF PARAELECTRIC MATERIAL CAN SENSE THE HEAT RADIATED BY A PERSON, AND THE ARRAY'S ELECTRICAL OUTPUTS PATTERN CAN THEN BE USED TO CONSTRUCT AN IMAGE. But until recently, no one bothered much with the reversal of this process. However, this inversion exists. Apply a suitable current to a parelectric material and it will cool. Someone looking at this opposite effect is Alex Mishenko, of Cambridge University. USING COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE PARAELECTRIC FILM, HE AND HIS COLLEAGUES CREATED TEMPERATURE DECLINES FIVE TIMES GREATER THAN ANYTHING PREVIOUSLY RECORDED. This may be enough to change the phenomenon from a laboratory curiosity to something with commercial applications. As for what those applications might be, Dr. Mishenko is still a bit vague. However, he formed a company to go after them. He anticipates using his discovery in more efficient household refrigerators and air conditioners. However, the real money may be in cooling computers. Gadgets containing microprocessors have been heating up for a long time. One of the results of Moore's Law, which describes the doubling of the number of transistors in a chip every 18 months, is that the amount of heat produced is also doubled. In fact, it more than doubles, because in addition to increasing their number, the components become faster. Heat is released whenever a sensible operation is performed inside a microprocessor, so the faster the processor, the more heat it produces. Doubling the frequency quadruples the heat output. And the frequency doubled a lot. The first Pentium chips sold by Dr. Moore's company, Intel, in 1993, went through 60 million cycles per second. The Pentium 4 - the latest CPU\ single-core\ desktop - moved 3.2 billion cycles per second. THIS HEAT DISSIPATION IS A MAJOR OBSTACLE TO FURTHER MINIMIZATION AND HIGHER SPEEDS. The inside of a desktop computer usually reaches 80C. At 85° C, they stop working. The adaptation of the processor heatsinks (copper or aluminum boxes designed to radiate heat) has reached its limit. So is adjusting the fans that distribute air above these heatsinks. And the idea of moving from processors with one core to systems that divide the processing power between first two subunits, and then four, in order to distribute the thermal load, also seems to be the end of the road in sight. One way out of this may be a second strange physical phenomenon, the thermoelectric effect. SIMILAR TO PARAELECTRIC MATERIALS, THIS GENERATES ELECTRICITY FROM A HEAT SOURCE AND GENERATES COOLING FROM AN ELECTRICAL SOURCE. Unlike parelectrics, a significant body of researchers is already working on it. THE TRICK TO A GOOD THERMOELECTRIC MATERIAL IS A CRYSTALLINE STRUCTURE IN WHICH ELECTRONS CAN FLOW FREELY, BUT THE PATH OF PHONONS - HEAT-CARRYING VIBRATIONS LARGER THAN ELECTRONS - IS CONSTANTLY DISTURBED. In practice, this trick is difficult to perform, so thermoelectric materials are less effective than preelectric ones (or, at least, than those tested by Dr. Mishenko). Nevertheless, Rama Vankatsubramanian, of Nextreme Thermal Solutions in North Carolina, claims to have manufactured thermoelectric refrigerators that can sit on the back of computer chips and cool hot spots at 10 degrees Celsius. Ali Shakuri, of the University of California, Santa Cruz, says his are even smaller - so small they can fit inside the chip. The last word in computer cooling, however, may shift to a system even less technical than a heat pump - a miniature version of a car radiator. Last year Apple launched a personal computer that is cooled by a liquid pumped through small channels in the processor, and from there to the radiator, where it gives up its heat to the atmosphere. To improve this, IBM's research lab in Zurich is experimenting with tiny jets that stimulate the liquid and thus make sure it all ends up touching the outside of the channel - the part where the heat exchange takes place. In the future, then, a combination of microchannels and thermoelectrics or parelectrics may cool computers. The old, as it were, hand in hand with the new.
hypothesis: IBM WILL ACHIEVE BETTER COMPUTER COOLING BY COMBINING MICROCHANNELS WITH PARAELECTRICS.

premise: Trade and the establishment of an early state Barter trade was a fundamental trade mechanism for many thousands of years; often sporadic and usually based on concepts of reciprocity, it involved the mutual exchange of goods or objects between individuals or groups. The redistribution of these goods through society was in the hands of chiefs, religious leaders or kin groups. Such redistribution was a fundamental component of kingdoms. The change from redistribution to formal trade that was often based on regulated commerce that may have included fixed prices and even currency was closely linked to the increasing political and social complexity and hence to the development of the state in the ancient world. In the 1970s, a number of archaeologists gave trade a major role in the rise of ancient states. British archaeologist Colin Renfrew attributed the dramatic flowering of Minoan civilization in Crete and through the Aegean Sea to boosting trade ties and to the impact of growing olives and vines on the local communities. As agricultural economies became more diverse and local food supplies could be purchased both locally and over longer distances, far-reaching economic interdependence was created. This eventually led to systems of redistribution of basic luxuries and goods, systems that were organized and controlled by Minoan rulers from their palaces. As time went on, the self-sufficiency of the communities was replaced by interdependence. The interest in long-distance trade brought a certain cultural homogeneity to trade and gift exchange, and may even have led to piracy. Thus, the increased trade and interaction, and the flourishing of specialist crafts, in a complex process of positive feedback, led to much more complex societies based on palaces, which were the economic centers of a new Minoan culture. Renfrew's model assumed some assumptions that have now been discounted. For example, he argued that the introduction of domesticated vines and olives enabled a significant expansion of lands in cultivation and helped drive the emergence of a complex society. Many archaeologists and paleobotanists now question this view, pointing out that the existing evidence for cultivated vines and olives suggests that they were only present in the later Bronze Age. Trade, however, was probably one of the many variables that led to the emergence of palace economies in Minoan Crete. AMERICAN ARCHAEOLOGIST WILLIAM RATJA DEVELOPED A HYPOTHESIS THAT SAW THE EXPLOSION IN LONG-DISTANCE EXCHANGES AS A FUNDAMENTAL CAUSE OF MAYAN CIVILIZATION IN MESOAMERICA. He suggested that the lowland Maya environment lacked many vital resources, among them obsidian, salt, stone for grinding corn, and many luxury materials. All these could be obtained from the nearby highlands, from the Valley of Mexico and other regions, if the necessary trading networks were created. Such ties, and the trading expeditions for their maintenance, could not be organized by individual villages. The Mayans lived in a relatively uniform environment, where each community suffered from the same resource deficiencies. Thus, Rataja argued, long-distance trade networks were organized through local ceremonial centers and their leaders. Over time, this organization became a state, and knowledge of its functioning was exportable, as were pottery, feathers of tropical birds, special stone materials and other local goods. Ratja's hypothesis probably explains part of the complex process of Mayan state formation, but it suffers from the resistance that suitable alternative raw materials can be found in the lowlands. It may also be that warfare became a competitive response to population growth and the increasing scarcity of primary agricultural lands, and that it played an important role in the emergence of the Mayan states.

premise: Trans fatty acids An editorial recently published in the British Medical Journal (BMJ), written by Oxford University researchers, called on food labels to list trans fats as well as cholesterol and saturated fat. Trans fats (or trans fatty acids) are a type of unsaturated fatty acid. They occur naturally in small amounts in foods produced from animals from Gira leaves such as milk, cattle, and lamb. However, most trans fatty acids on the menu are produced through the process of partial hydrogenation (hardening) of vegetable oils into semi-solid fats. They are therefore found in hard margarines, partially hydrogenated cooking oils, and in some bakery products, fried foods and other processed foods produced using these. Trans fatty acids have a negative effect on certain chemicals, called fats, that are found in the blood and have been shown to increase the risk of heart disease. They also raise LDL cholesterol (the bad cholesterol) and lower HDL cholesterol (the good cholesterol). They may also have adverse effects on the risk of cardiovascular disease that are independent of the effect on blood lipids (Mozaffarian et al. 2006). In a recent review of prospective studies examining the effects of trans fatty acids, a 2% increase in energy intake from trans fatty acids was linked to a 23% increase in the incidence of heart disease. The authors also reported that the negative effects of trans fatty acids were observed even at very low intake (3% of total daily energy intake, or about 2—7 g/day) (Mozaffarian et al. 2006). However, in this latest review only trans fatty acids produced during the hardening of vegetable oils are found to be harmful to health. The public health implications of trans fatty acid consumption from Gira products are thought to be relatively limited. Over the past decade, population consumption of trans fatty acids in the UK has declined and is now, on average, well below 2% of the total recommended energy set by the Department of Health in 1991, at 1.2% of energy (Henderson et al. 2003). This is not to say that trans fatty acid intake is not still a problem, and dietary advice states that those people who are at the upper end of the consumption distribution should still make efforts to reduce their intake. Currently, trans fatty acids in foods are labeled in the US, but not in the UK and Europe. The UK Food Standards Agency (FSA) supports amending the European directive governing the content and format of food labels so that trans fatty acids are labelled. This should enable consumers to make better food choices when it comes to heart health (Clarke & Lewington 2006). Recognizing the negative health effects of trans fatty acids, many food manufacturers and retailers have been systematically removing them from their products in recent years. For example, they have long been absent from major brands of margarine and other fat spreads, which are now produced in a different technique. Also, many companies now have guidelines that lead to the reformulation and reduction or elimination of trans fatty acids in products where they were previously found, such as snack products, fried products, and baked goods. As a result, the vast majority of salty and crunchy biscuits produced in the UK do not contain partially hydrogenated oils. Similarly, changes are made to the way bakery products are manufactured. For example, a leading European maker of major brands of biscuits, cakes and snacks recently announced that these are now produced without partially hydrogenated vegetable oils, a transition that began in 2004. Alongside these changes, the manufacturer also reported a cut in the amount of saturates. It is clear that a key technical challenge in achieving such changes is simply avoiding the substitution of trans fatty acids for saturated fatty acids, which also have harmful health effects. Foods marked as containing oils or partially hydrogenated fats are a source of trans fatty acids (sometimes partially hydrogenated fats are only labeled as hydrogenated fats). These foods include hard margarines, some fried products and some manufactured bakery products such as biscuits, pastries, and cakes. It is important to note that consumption may have changed in light of the reformulation of foods that has taken place over the past six years in the UK, as stated earlier. premise: Plants transgenic genes from almost every organism, from viruses to humans, can now be inserted into plants, creating what are known as transgenic plants. Currently used in agriculture, there are about 109 million acres of transgenic crops grown worldwide, 68 percent of them in the United States. The most common transgenic crops are soybeans, corn, cotton, and canola. Most often, these plants contain a gene that makes them resistant to the herbicide glyphosate or they contain an insect-resistant gene that produces a protein called Bt toxin. On the plus side, advocates of transgenic crops argue that these crops are environmentally friendly because they allow farmers to use fewer and fewer harmful chemicals to produce crops. For example, a 21 percent reduction in insecticide use was reported on Bt cotton (engineered cotton that produces Bt toxin). In addition, when glyphosate is used for weed control, it is not necessary to apply other, more persistent herbicides. On the negative side, opponents of transgenic crops suggest that there are many questions that need to be answered before growing large-scale transgenic crops. One question deals with the effects that Bt plants have on non-target organisms such as beneficial insects, worms, and birds that consume the genetically modified crop. For example, monarch larvae feeding on milkweed plants near Bt corn fields will eat some corn pollen that has fallen on milkweed leaves. Laboratory studies indicate that larvae can die from eating Bt pollen. However, field tests indicate that Bt corn is not likely to harm monarchs. Furthermore, pesticide application (the alternative to growing Bt plants) has been shown to cause extensive damage to non-target insects. Another unanswered question is whether herbicide-resistant genes will pass into weed populations. Crop plants are sometimes grown in areas where weedy relatives also live. If the crop plants hybridize and multiply with weedy relatives, then this herbicide-resistant gene will be immortalized in the offspring. In this way the resistant gene can work its way into the weed population. If this happens, a farmer can no longer use glyphosate, for example, to kill these weeds. This scenario is unlikely to occur in many cases because there are no weedy relatives growing near the crop plant. However, in some cases, it may turn into a serious problem. For example, canola hybridizes easily with mustard herb species and can transfer the herbicide-resistant genes to those weeds. We know that evolution will occur when transgenic plants grow on a large scale over a period of time. Of particular concern is the development of insect populations resistant to the Bt toxin. This pesticide has been applied to plants for decades without the development of insect-resistant populations. However, transgenic Bt plants express the toxin in all tissues throughout the growing season. Therefore, all insects carrying genes that make them susceptible to the toxin will die. This leaves only the genetically resistant insects alive to perpetuate the population. When these resistant insects mate, they will produce a high proportion of offspring capable of surviving in the presence of the toxin Bt. Farmers are trying to slow the development of insect resistance in Bt crops by, for example, planting non-engineered border rows to provide a haven for susceptible insects. These insects may allow Bt susceptibility to remain in the population. Perhaps the most serious concern about the transgenic crop plants currently in use is that they encourage farmers to move away from sustainable farming methods, that is, those that allow natural resources to be continually replenished in the long term. Transgenes, at least superficially, simplify agriculture by narrowing the choices made by the executive. Planting a glyphosate-resistant crop requires the farmer to use this herbicide for the season, probably excluding all other herbicides and other weed control methods. Farmers using Bt transgenicity may not feel they need to follow integrated pest management practices that use beneficial insects and timely applications of pesticides to control insect pests. A more sustainable approach would be to plant unmodified corn, monitor the fields throughout the growing season and then apply pesticide only if necessary.
hypothesis: Planting non-engineered plants alongside Bt plants may help Bt sensitive insects remain part of the population.

premise: Trending in the Indian fashion and textile industry during the 1950s, the Indian fashion scene was exciting, stylish and very graceful. There were no celebrity designers or models, nor were there widely recognized labels. The value of a garment is judged by its style and fabric rather than by who made it. It is considered perfectly acceptable, even for women in high society, to turn to an unknown tailor who can make an outfit for a few rupees, providing the perfect fit, finish and style. They were proud to achieve a bargain, and give their own name to the end result. The Sixties were an era full of mischief and celebration in art, music and film. The period was marked by freedom from restrictions, and in the fashion world, the acceptance of innovative types of materials such as plastic and coated polyester. Tight kurtas and chorizers and high hair were a trend among women. The following decade witnessed an increase in the export of traditional materials, and the arrival of international fashion to India. Synthetics became trendy, and disco culture influenced the fashion scene. It was in the early 80s when the first Ravissant fashion store opened in Mumbai. At the time, clothes were sold for a four-figure price tag. American designers such as Calvin Klein have become popular. In India, too, the contours became more masculine, and even the Salwar Kameez was designed with shoulder pads. With the development of designer stores came the culture of designer fashion, along with its hefty price tags. Whatever the garment was, consumers were convinced that a higher price tag signified elegant designer fashion, so clothes sold at unbelievable prices. Meanwhile, designers decided to pay attention to themselves by making extravagant outfits and connecting with the right celebrities. Soon, fashion shows became competitive, each designer tried to outdo the other in the subject, guest list and media coverage. In the last decade of the millennium, the market has narrowed and ethnic attire has made a comeback. During the recession there was a push to sell at any price. With stiff competition the inevitable occurred: the once-heavy price tags began their downward journey, and the fashion show industry followed suit. However, the vitality of the Indian fashion scene has not ended it has only just reached a steady level. premise: UK companies need more effective boards After a number of serious governance failures (i.e., how they are run at the highest level), companies in the UK, as well as elsewhere, need to consider radical changes to the roles of their directors. It is clear that the role of a board director today is not easy. Following the financial meltdown of 2008, which resulted in a deeper and more prolonged period of economic decline than anyone had expected, the search for explanations in the many aftermaths of the crisis resulted in the blame being spread all over the world. Governments, regulators, central banks and auditors have all been in the frame. The role of bank executives and management and their famous failures have been selected and examined extensively in reports, inquiries and commentaries. The countervailing effect of this scrutiny was to make the governance of the companies in general a subject of intense public debate and significantly increased the pressures on directors and their responsibilities. At the simplest and most practical level, the time involved in fulfilling board requirements has increased significantly, which has called into question the effectiveness of the classic model of corporate governance by independent directors who are not part-time executives. Where once a board's schedule consisted of between eight and ten meetings a year, in many companies the number of events requiring board inputs and decisions has risen dramatically. Moreover, the amount of reading and preparation required for each meeting is increasing. The agenda can be overloaded and it may mean that the time for constructive debate must be limited in favour of moving beyond business. Often, board business is transferred to committees in order to handle the workload, which may be more effective but can result in the board as a whole being less involved in fully handling some of the most important issues. It is not uncommon for an audit committee meeting to last longer than the main board meeting itself. The process may take the place of debate and be at the expense of genuine cooperation, so that boxes are ticked rather than addressing issues. A radical solution, which may work for some very large companies whose businesses are extensive and complex, is the professional board, whose members will work up to three or four days a week, with the support of their own dedicated staff and consultants. There are clear risks to this and it is important to set clear guidelines for such a board to ensure it does not tread on management's fingers by becoming too preoccupied with the day-to-day running of the company. Recruitment, remuneration and independence problems may also arise and this structure will not be suitable for all companies. However, more professional and informed boards were particularly suited to banks where directors had access to information lacking for part-time non-executive directors, leaving the latter unable to understand or anticipate the crash of 2008. One of the main criticisms of their boards and directors is that they do not focus enough on long-term issues of strategy, sustainability and governance, but concentrate too much on short-term financial indicators. Regulatory requirements and market structure encourage this behavior. The tyranny of quarterly reporting could distort board decision-making, because directors have to “do the numbers” every four months to meet the market's insatiable appetite for more data. This serves to encourage the trading methodology of a particular type of investor who enters and exits a stock without engaging in a constructive dialogue with the company about strategy or performance, and simply looking for short-term financial gain. This effect has been exacerbated by the changing profile of investors due to the globalization of capital and the increasing use of automated trading systems. The corporate culture adapts and management teams are largely encouraged to meet financial objectives. Compensation for CEOs has become a fighting zone where battles are being waged between investors, management and board members, often behind closed doors but more and more often in the full glow of journalistic attention. Many would argue that it is in the interest of transparency and good governance because shareholders use their muscle in the area of pay to pressure boards to remove low-performing CEOs. Their powers to vote against executives' remuneration policies increased with the entry into force of binding votes. Chairing the remuneration committee can be a bare and lonely role, as Alison Carnwath, chair of Barclays Bank's remuneration committee, discovered when she was forced to resign, after being strongly criticised for trying to protect the huge bonus to be paid to the chief executive; the irony is that she is widely understood to have spoken out against him in private the committee. The financial crisis sparked debate about the role and purpose of the company and increased awareness of corporate ethics. Trust in the corporation is eroding and academics such as Michael Sandell, in his calculated and bestselling book What Money Can't Buy, are questioning the morality of capitalism and market economics. Boards of directors of companies in all sectors will need to broaden their perspective to encompass these issues and this may involve a re-adjustment of the company's objectives. We live in challenging times.
hypothesis: Using a committee structure will ensure that board members are fully informed about significant issues.
label: c

premise: UK Rail Services How do I claim my delayed train? Generally, if you've been delayed travelling on a train, you may be able to claim compensation, but train companies have different rules, so it can be confusing to work out what you're entitled to. The type of delay you can claim for depends on whether the rail company runs a delay reimbursement scheme or a less generous, older-style scheme. Delay reimbursement is a train operators' scheme to compensate passengers when trains are late, and the rail company would pay even if it was not responsible for the delay. The plan varies between companies, but by 2016 most were paying 50 percent of the cost of the individual ticket for a 30-minute delay and 100 percent for an hour. On the London Underground, you get a full refund for 15-minute delays. Companies that do not use Delay Return and still use the older scheme will not generally pay compensation if the problem is deemed out of their control. But it is still worth asking them for compensation, since some of them may pay. You are unlikely to receive compensation for delay if any of the following occur: accidents where people come on the line illegally Gas leaks or fires in buildings adjacent to the line not caused by a train company Line closures at the request of the emergency services Extremely severe weather conditions Strike action National Railways conditions of travel state that you are entitled to compensation in the same way you paid for the ticket. Some train companies still pay using train vouchers, which they are allowed to do if you don't ask for a refund. Since 2016, rail passengers have acquired additional rights to compensation through the Consumer Rights Act. This means passengers can now be entitled to compensation due to: a very crowded train with too few cars available; a consistently late service; and a service that is delayed less than the time limit that applies under existing compensation schemes. However, in order to exercise their rights beyond existing compensation schemes, for example repayment deferrals, and when the train operating company refuses to compensate despite letters threatening court action, passengers may have to submit their claims to a court.
hypothesis: Under delay reimbursement, a train company would only provide compensation if it caused a delay.

premise: Skin removal If you take off your skin and lay it flat, it will cover an area of about twenty-one square meters, making it by far the largest organ in the body. Wrapped in place on our bodies, skin forms the barrier between what's inside us and what's outside. It protects us from a lot of external forces. It serves as an avenue to our most intimate physical and psychological selves. This opaque but permeable barrier, less than a millimeter thick in places, consists of three layers. The outermost layer is the bloodless epidermis. The dermis includes collagen, elastin and nerve endings. The innermost layer, subcutaneous fat, contains tissue that serves as an energy source, cushion and insulator for the body. From these familiar characteristics of the skin arises the deep mystery of touch, without a doubt our most essential source of sensory stimulation. We can live without actually seeing or hearing, without any of our other senses. But babies born without effective neural connections between skin and brain may not thrive and may even die. Laboratory experiments decades ago, now considered unethical and inhumane, prevented baby monkeys from being touched by their mothers. It did not matter that the babies could see, hear and smell their mothers; without touching the babies became apathetic and unable to progress. For humans, insufficient contact in the early years can cause lifelong consequences. In touch-touching cultures, adults' aggression is low, while in cultures where contact is limited, adults' aggression is high, writes Tiffany Field, director of the Touch Research Institutes at the University of Miami School of Medicine. Studies of a variety of cultures show a correlation between high rates of childhood physical affection and low rates of adult physical violence. While the effects of touching are easy to understand, the mechanics of it are less so. Your skin has millions of nerve cells in different shapes at different depths, explains Stanley Bolanowski, a neuroscientist and associate director of the Institute for Sensory Research at Syracuse University. When nerve cells are stimulated, the physical energy becomes energy used by the nervous system and is transferred from the skin to the spinal cord and brain. It's called transduction, and no one knows exactly how it occurs. Suffice it to say that the process involves the complex action of a fraction of a second of a complex system of signals between neurons in the skin and brain. This starts to sound very confusing until Bulnovsky says: Simply put, people perceive three basic things through the skin: pressure, temperature, and pain. And then I'm sure he's wrong. When I get wet, my skin feels wet, I protest. Close your eyes and lean back, says Bulanowski. Something cold and wet is on my forehead so wet, in fact, that I'm waiting for the water to start dripping down my cheeks. Open your eyes. Bolnovsky says and shows me that the feeling comes from a chilled, but dry roll of metal. The combination of stress and cold, he explains, is what makes my skin catch moisture. He gives me a surgical glove to wear and makes me put a finger in a glass of cold water. My finger feels wet, even though I have visual proof that it doesn't touch the water. My skin, which seems so reliable, has been fooling me all my life. When I shower or wash my hands, I realize now, my skin feels pressure and temperature. My brain says I feel wet. Perceptions of pressure, temperature, and pain manifest themselves in many different ways. Gentle stimulation of pressure receptors can cause tickling; subtle irritation of pain receptors, itching. Both sensations arise from neurological transmission, not from something that physically exists. The skin, I understand, is under constant assault, both from within the body and from outside forces. Repairs occur with varying success. Take the place where I cut myself with a knife while cutting fruit. I have a crunchy scab surrounded by pink tissue about a quarter of an inch long in the palm of my right hand. Under the scab, epidermal cells migrate into the wound to close it. Once the process is complete, the scab will fall off to reveal a new epidermis. It's only been a few days, but my little self-correction is almost complete. Similarly, we recover quickly from minor burns. If you ever touch a hot burner, just put your finger in cold water. Chances are you won't have a blister, little pain and no scar. Severe burns, however, are another matter.
hypothesis: The skin is more sensitive to pressure than to temperature or pain.
label: n

premise: Under the law, negligence is usually defined in the context of jury instructions in which a judge instructs the jury that a party will be considered negligent if he does not exercise the standard of care that a reasonable person would have exercised in the same circumstances. In most jurisdictions, it is first necessary to show that a person had a duty to exercise caution in a given situation, and that he violated that duty. In short: negligence, tort, is a civil error consisting of five criteria: duty or reasonable level of care (as decided by the judge as a matter of law), violation (or negligence in layman's terms, decided in practice), injury (the fact that the plaintiff was harmed, and determined in practice), actual cause or conduct of the defendant causing the plaintiff injury (duly decided) a matter of fact), legal cause (currently seen as a prediction of the type of harm caused but not the specific harm or extent of the harm, determined as a matter of fact). Matters of law are determined by a judge, matters of fact are determined by a jury. In order to prove negligence, it is not necessary to prove damage, but in order for a cause of action to remain in tort, damage must be proved. Accordingly, it would be meaningless to sue someone for negligence if no harm was caused. Conversely, it is not enough damage has been caused. International students are represented by an Overseas Student Officer, a part-time position in the union. Alumni Association All graduate students at St. James University are automatically members of the Alumni Association. It plays an important role in representing the interests of all graduate students, and also serves as a social club. The Alumni Association annually elects international officers who represent the interests of students from Europe and outside Europe. premise: Urban planning in Singapore British merchants established a trading post in Singapore in the early nineteenth century, and for more than a century dominated commercial interests. However, in 1965 the newly independent island state was cut off from its neck, so it began to resort to a survival strategy. The good international media it already enjoyed provided a useful foundation, but it was decided that if Singapore was to secure its economic future, it should develop its industry. For this, new institutional structures were needed to facilitate, develop and control foreign investment. One of the most important of these was the Economic Development Council (EDB), a government arm that developed strategies for attracting investment. This is how from the outset the Singapore government was involved in promoting the city. Towards the end of the twentieth century, the government realized that due to limitations in both the size of the country's workforce and its land area, its labor-intensive industries were becoming increasingly uncompetitive. So an economic committee was formed which concluded that Singapore should focus on development as a service centre, and seek to attract the company's headquarters to serve Southeast Asia, and develop tourism, banking and foreign affairs activities. The land required for this orientation of the service sector was acquired in the early 1970s, when the government realized that it lacked the banking infrastructure for a modern economy. A new banking and corporate district was then planned, known as the Golden Slipper, incorporating the historic commercial area. This district currently houses all major companies and various government financial agencies. Singapore's current economic strategy is closely related to land use and development planning. Although it is already a major city, the current development plan seeks to ensure the continued economic growth of Singapore through restructuring, to ensure that the facilities needed for future businesses are now planned. These include transport and telecommunications infrastructure, land and the environment. A key concern is to prevent congestion in the central area, so the latest plan deviates from previous plans by a strong decentralization policy. The plan establishes four major regional centers, each of which serves 800,000 people, but this does not mean that the existing central business district will not grow either. A major expansion planned around Marina Bay rests on examples of other world cities, particularly those with key waterside areas like Sydney and San Francisco. The project involves a large land reclamation of 667 hectares in total. Part of this has already been developed as a conference and exhibition area, and the rest will be used for other facilities. However, the need for vitality was recognised and a mixed zoning approach was adopted, which would include housing and entertainment. One of the new features of the current program is a broader conception of what contributes to economic success. It encompasses the provision of high quality living, good environment, leisure facilities and exciting city life. Hence there is more supply for low-density housing, often in communities on the waterfront linked to beaches and recreation facilities. However, the low housing density will put considerable pressure on the very limited land available for development, and this creates problems for other objectives of the plan, which is highlighting environmentalism. More and more of the remaining open space will be developed, and the only surviving natural landscape will be a small area in the centre of the island used as a water catchment area. Environmental policy is therefore very concerned with making the built environment greener by introducing more plants what is known as Singapore beautification. The plan focuses on green areas that define the boundaries of settlements, and on the way to transport corridors. The accompanying green supply in the housing areas also receives a lot of attention. Much of the environmental supply, for example golf courses, recreation areas and beaches, is related to the main purpose of attracting business. The plan places great emphasis on providing good leisure and the need to take advantage of Singapore's island environment. One way to do this is through further land reclamation, creating an entirely new island dedicated to leisure and luxury housing that will stretch from the main area to the airport. A contemporary concern also seems to be how to use the planning system to create opportunities for greater spontaneity: planners have recently paid close attention to the concept of the 24-hour city and the coffee shop company. For example, an operation took place along the Singapore River to create a cafe area. This included the realisation, rather late in the day, of the value of retaining older buildings, and the creation of a continuous riverside promenade. Since the relaxation in 1996 of strict guidelines on outdoor eating areas, it has become an extremely popular area in the evenings. Also in 1998, the Urban Redevelopment Authority established a new downtown recreation area, which they promote as the city's dynamic entertainment scene. In summary, Singapore's economic development has been very consciously planned centrally, and the latest strategy is clearly aimed at establishing Singapore as a leading global city. She is well placed to succeed, for a variety of reasons. It can tap into its historical roots as a global trade center; it has invested heavily in telecommunications and air transport infrastructure; it is well positioned relative to other Asian economies; it has developed a safe and clean environment; and it has utilized the international language of English.
hypothesis: Singapore will find it difficult to compete with leading cities in other regions of the world.

premise: Vertical transport and a death-defying stunt that shaped the skyline of the world A can be traced back to the raising of water from a well using a bucket suspended from a rope since ancient times. The method could be improved by attaching an empty bucket to the opposite end of the rope, then lowering it down the well as the full bucket rose, to balance the weight. To overcome the problem, lower a basket to the base of the cliff at the end of a rope coiled around a wooden pole, known as winglass. It was possible to lift heavy weights with the help of a windwheel, especially if a small cogwheel on the crankshaft drove a larger cogwheel on a second rod. Materials and people were hoisted in this way, but it was a slow process and if the rope was breaking the basket dropped to the ground. C In the mid-nineteenth century the general public viewed rope-supported elevators as too dangerous for personal use. Without an elevator, the height of a commercial building was limited by the number of stairs that one could expect people to climb in an economic time period. It was the American inventor and manufacturer Elisha Graves Otis (181161) who finally solved the problem of passenger elevators. D In 1852, Otis pioneered the idea of a safety brake, and two years later he displayed it spectacularly at the Crystal Palace Industrial Exposition in New York. Otis stood on the lifting platform, four stories above an expectant crowd. The rope was cut, and after a little jolt, the platform stopped. Otis stunts boosted people's confidence in elevators and sales increased. E THE OPERATING PRINCIPLE OF THE SAFETY ELEVATOR WAS DESCRIBED AND ILLUSTRATED IN ITS PATTERN DOCUMENTATION FROM 1861. The lifting platform was suspended between two vertical pillars each lined with a jagged guide rail. A hook was placed on the sides of the platform to connect to the teeth, allowing vertical upward but not downward movement. The lift descent was only possible if the hooks were pulled inward, which could only happen when the rope was in tension. If the rope had broken, the tension would be lost and the hooks would jump out to engage the teeth and stop the fall. Modern elevators incorporate similar safety mechanisms. F Otis installed the first passenger elevator in a New York store in 1957. Following the success of the elevator, taller buildings were built, and sales grew again as the business expanded into Europe. The first Otis passenger elevator in England (or elevator as the British say) appeared four years later with the opening of the London Grosvenor Hotel. More significantly perhaps, the advent of passenger elevators marked the birth of the modern skyscraper. G passenger elevators were operated by steam before 1902. A rope carrying the cab was wrapped around a rotating drum driven by a steam engine. The method was too slow for a tall building, which needed a large drum to hold a long rope reel. The following year, Otis developed a compact electric tow lift that used cable but eliminated the winding gears, allowing the passenger cabin to be raised over 100 stories quickly and efficiently. H In the electric lift, the cable was routed from the top of the passenger compartment to a pulley at the top of the lifting shaft then back down to a weight used as a counterbalance. An electric gear motor rotates the pulley wheel, which contained a slot for gripping the cable and providing the traction. Following the success of the electric elevator, high-rise buildings began to emerge in major cities. The Woolworths building in New York City, built in 1913, was a significant land mark, being the tallest building in the world for the next 27 years. It had 57 floors and the fast Otis electric elevators could reach the top floor in just over one minute. I Each elevator used several cables and pulley wheels, although one cable was enough to support the weight of the car. As an added safety feature, an oil-filled shock piston was installed at the base of the lifting shaft to act as a buffer, slowing the car at a safe pace in the unlikely event of any cable as well as the safety brake.

premise: Video Game Research Although video games were first developed for adults, they are no longer reserved exclusively for adults at home. Mobile Systems has done a particularly good job of penetrating the young market. Research in the video game market is usually done in two stages: some time near the end of the product cycle, in order to get feedback from consumers, so that a marketing strategy can be developed; and at the end of the product cycle to correct bugs in the game. While both of these types of research are important, and may be appropriate for dealing with older consumers, neither helps design better games, especially when it comes to designing for an audience that may have particular needs, such as preschoolers or senior citizens. Instead, exploratory and formative research should be undertaken in order to truly understand those audiences, their abilities, their perspective, and their needs. In the spring of 2007, the production team of our preschool games at Nickelodeon had the feeling that the Nintendo DS with its new features, such as the microphone, small size and mobility, and its relatively low price point was a gaming platform ripe for preschoolers. There were some games on the market at the time that had characters that appealed to the younger set, but our game producers didn't think the game mechanics or design were appropriate for preschoolers. What exactly preschoolers could do with the system, however, was a bit of a mystery. So we began conducting research to answer the query: What might we expect preschoolers to be capable of in the context of manual play, and how might the child development literature inform us as we continue to create a new outlet for this age group? Our context in this case was the United States, although the resulting games were also released in other regions, due to the wide international reach of the characters. In order to design the best possible DS product for a preschool audience we were absolutely committed to the ideals of a user-centric approach, which assumes that users are at least considered, but ideally advised in the development process. After all, when it comes to introducing a new interactive product to the children's market, and especially such a young age group within it, we believe that it is essential to assess the range of physical and cognitive abilities associated with their specific stage of development. Revelle and Medoff (2002) review some of the fundamental reasons why home entertainment systems, computers, and other electronic gaming devices are often difficult to use in early childhood. In addition to the still-developing motor skills (the keys to manipulating a controller with small buttons), many of the main stumbling blocks are cognitive. Although preschoolers learn to think symbolically, realizing that pictures can be objects in real life, the vast majority are still unable to read and write. Thus, using text-based menu choices is unsustainable. Mapping is another obstacle because preschoolers may not realize that there is a direct relationship between how the controller is used and the activities that appear in front of them on the screen. Although this aspect varies, in traditional mapping systems real life movements are not usually translated into game-based activity. In the course of our research, we gained many insights into how preschoolers interact with various platforms, including the DS. For example, all instructions for preschoolers need to be in voice, and include visual representations, and that was one of the most difficult areas for us to negotiate in relation to game design on the DS. Because game cartridges have very limited memory capacity, especially compared to console or PC games, the ability to capture large amounts of sound data using sound files or visual representations of instructions becomes limited. Text instructions occupy minimal memory, so they are preferable from a technological point of view. Finding ways to maximize sound and graphics files, while maintaining the clear visual and verbal cues that we know are critical for our youngest players, is a constant give-and-take. Another of our findings indicated that preschoolers may use a pen, or their fingers, or both even though they are not very accurate with either. One of the very interesting aspects of the DS is that the interface, designed to respond to stylus interactions, can be effectively used even with the fingertip. This is particularly notable in the context of preschoolers for two reasons. First, because they have difficulty with fine motor skills and their hand-eye coordination is still developing, they are less precise in their stylus movements; and second, their fingers are so small that they mimic the stylus very effectively, so by using their fingers they can often be more precise in their game interactions.

premise: Vitamins to add or not? Mineral health supplements, vitamins, and antioxidants make up a multibillion-dollar industry in the United States alone, but do they really work? Evidence suggests that a supplement is clearly indicated in special circumstances, but can actually be harmful in others. In the pursuit of a longer, happier and healthier life, there are certainly better investments for most people than a pipeline of vitamin supplements. Certain subgroups of the population can gain proven benefit from supplements. Folic acid has long been indicated as a prenatal supplement due to its assistance in the division of fetal cells and the corresponding ability to prevent birth defects in the neural tube. Since Canada and the United States decided to require fortifying white flour with folic acid, spinal birth defects have plummeted by 75%, and rates of neuroblastoma (a devastating form of infant cancer) are now 50% lower. In countries without such fortification, or for women on low-carb diets, a prenatal multivitamin can make the crucial difference. The United States Department of Health and Human Services concluded that the elderly may also benefit from vitamin D supplementation; calcium can help prevent bone fractures; and zinc and antioxidants can maintain vision while diverting macular degeneration in people who would otherwise be likely to develop this affliction. However, there is increasing evidence for many people to stay away from multivitamins. The National Institutes of Health noted disturbing evidence of risk among tobacco users: beta-carotene, a common ingredient in multivitamins, was found during a six-year study to be a significant contributor to higher lung cancer and mortality rates among smokers. Meanwhile, excessive vitamin A (a supplement often taken to boost the immune system) has been shown to increase women's risk of hip fracture, and vitamin E, thought to improve cardiovascular health, was not countered in a study that proved higher rates of heart failure among users of such vitamins. Antioxidant supplementation has no purpose and accomplishes nothing, according to the Food and Nutrition Board of the National Academy of Sciences, and the Medical Letters Group went so far as to suggest they may interfere with treatment and promote some cancers. Antioxidants are generally thought to counteract the destructive effect of free radicals in the body, but according to the medical letters theory, free radicals may also serve the purpose of sending a powerful signal to the body's immune system to repair the damage. By taking supplements, we risk undermining this message and disrupting the balance of antioxidants and free radicals in the body. The supplements counteract the free radicals, the immune system is not placed on alert, and the disease can sneak through the gates. One problem with supplements in tablets is the poor track record in digestion. These tablets are often equipped with metal-based minerals that are basically miniature rocks, and our body is unable to digest them. Even the vitamin elements of these theoretically digestible pills are often not able to be extracted efficiently by our body when they arrive in such a concentrated form. In Salt Lake City, for example, over 150 gallons of vitamin and mineral pellets are collected from the sewer filters every month. According to the doctors' table, only about 10% 20% of multivitamins are absorbed by the body. The National Advisory Council is even more damning, suggesting that each 100 mg tablet corresponds to about 8.3 mg of blood concentration, though notes that it can still play a beneficial role in some cases. Due to its aesthetic appeal, water hyacinth, which originated in South America, has been distributed to many different regions and is now thriving in the southern states of the US and in many subtropical and tropical locations. It has also been observed to be relatively tolerant of cooler climates and is routinely sold as an ornamental plant for home use in a number of horticultural centers. ALTHOUGH THE HYACINTH SPECIES IS DISTINCT IN APPEARANCE, ANOTHER AQUATIC WATER PLANT FLOATING WATER LETTUCE IS SOMETIMES MISTAKENLY IDENTIFIED AS WATER HYACINTH. However, water lettuce does not have the same attractive flowers, has larger leaves and is less tolerant of cooler climates. Water hyacinth has rounded, green waxy leaves that grow to about 6 inches across and floating leaf stalks that grow up to 12 inches long. The width of the flowers is usually between 2 and 3 inches and up to 15 flowers, each purple on the outside and containing a yellow center, may grow from each plant. Many of the problems associated with water hyacinth stem from its remarkable growth and reproductive abilities, which have made it difficult to control and allow it to quickly dominate the environment in which it grows and spreads. Its growth patterns are characterized by the rapid formation of an impermeable vegetation mass; botanists say one plant can produce about 5000 seeds and in one study two plants were observed producing 1200 plants in just 4 months. Following nature's usual pattern, water hyacinth seeds are distributed outside the immediate area by bird, animal, wind, and water streams, facilitating growth in surrounding areas that were previously free of the plant. Control of environments by water hyacinth populations has a number of negative consequences. For humans, difficulties may be encountered in moving boats through areas of rivers and lakes where the plant is present and fishing and swimming opportunities may be limited. However, the implications for the ecosystem of the immediate environment may be even more worrying. The mass density of water hyacinth populations can prevent adequate amounts of sunlight and oxygen from reaching the water: as a result, significant numbers of fish may die, other species of plants growing below the surface of the water are damaged and therefore the ecosystem of the immediate area can be unbalanced. Furthermore, the conditions created by the presence of water hyacinth, although harmful to most life forms, are perfect for encouraging the growth of deadly bacteria that are often found in poorly oxygenated areas of water. In the southern states of the US, in Florida in particular, water hyacinth is currently under maintenance control. The plant population can be limited in several ways: including the use of herbicides, evacuation equipment, and biological pest control insects. However, efforts to minimize the water hyacinth population need to be sustained and consistent; experts warn that unless control methods are maintained, the problem could easily return. Some say that inattention to a twelve-month period would allow numbers to quickly return to the contagion level; hardly surprising given that the species is known to be able to multiply in just 12 days. Water hyacinth is thought to have been introduced to Africa in the 1800s; its presence in Lake Kyoga was first identified in 1988 and in Lake Victoria in 1989. In the mid-1990s, it was estimated that water hyacinth controls 10% of the waters of the latter lakes. However, by 1998, the plant had been almost completely eradicated from East African waters; this is mainly achieved by the use of biological control insects, in this case snout beetles, a type of weevil that feeds only on water hyacinth plant species. Tens of thousands of weevils were distributed throughout the lake regions of East Africa, their habit of feeding on the leaves and laying their eggs in the stems of the plants eventually causing the plants to die and sink to the bottom of the lake. In addition, the plant population was removed using mechanical cleaning equipment and by hand with a machete. Despite the earlier success, however, negative consequences of human activity prompted the return of water hyacinth to East African waters. Uganda's Lake Kyoga, has recently again experienced problems with infestation. Sewage and agricultural waste that make their way into the waterways and thus create an excess of nutrients in the water have been the main contributing factors to the re-emergence of water hyacinth. In addition, high levels of nitrogen in rainfall, which enters the water cycle from the smoke generated by cooking fires in wood used in the area, also serve as nutrition for the growing plant population. Limiting human activity in such lakes, caused by the spread of water hyacinth, has enormous consequences; villages like Kayago, which is in close proximity to the lake, are often almost entirely dependent on fishing activities for their economy and food source. While the spread of water hyacinth in Lake Victoria at the time of writing stands at 0.5%, well below the 10% level experienced in the mid-1990s, experts fear that growth may once again spiral out of control. The main concern is that as a result of changing weather conditions, the activity of the snout beetle may be less effective than in the past. The area around Lake Victoria experiences a prolonged period of drought and while the water hyacinth is able to live and reproduce both in lakes and on surrounding land, its predator, the snout beetle can only survive on water. Plant populations growing in lakeside locations are therefore under limited threat from the insect brought in to control them and are consequently able to reproduce with relative freedom.

premise: Desert weathering In deserts, as elsewhere, rocks on earth are altered by weathering, which may be defined as the disintegration of rocks in the place they reside. Weathering processes are chemical, when it comes to the alteration of some of the constituent particles; or mechanical, when there is only physical disintegration and fragmentation of rocks. Which process will dominate depends primarily on the mineralogy and texture of the rock and the local climate, but several individual processes usually work together to the common end of the rock's disintegration. The large daily changes in the temperature of deserts have long been thought to be responsible for the disintegration of rocks, either by differential heating of the various minerals that form rock or by differential heating between the outer and inner parts of the rock masses. However, both field observations and laboratory experiments have led to a reassessment of the importance of sun exposure in desert weathering. Nearly half a century ago Burton remarked that the buried parts of some of Egypt's ancient monuments had more stamps than those parts fully exposed to the sun's rays, attributing this to the effects of subsurface water absorption. Laboratory experiments have shown that rocks exposed to many cycles of large temperature fluctuations (larger than those experienced in nature) show no evidence of fragmentation or fragmentation, as a result. However, when considerable temperature fluctuations occur in humid conditions small rock fragments quickly form. It has often been argued that the broad action of crystallizing salts exerts sufficient force to break up rocks. Few would dispute that this mechanism is capable of disrupting fragile or well-fractured rocks or boulders already weakened by other weathering agencies; split wood, crumbling terracotta tiles and clay is disturbed by the mechanism, but its importance when acting on fresh, cohesive crystalline rocks remains uncertain. Weathering achieves more than the disintegration of rocks, although this is its most important geomorphic effect. This causes the development of specific land forms. Many rocks have a superficial hard layer of iron oxide and/or silica, substances which have migrated in solution from the inside of the block towards the surface. Not only does the exterior harden, but the depleted interior crumbles easily. When weathering penetrates the shell the inner part is quickly attacked and only the hard outer layer is left to give hollow rocks or deer. Another superficial layer, the exact nature of which is little understood, is a well-known desert varnish or patina, a glossy coat over rocks and pebbles and characteristic of arid environments. Some varnishes are colorless, others are light brown, but others are so dark that they are almost black. Its origin is unknown but it is significant, since it has been suggested that lacquer darkens with the passage of time; it is clear that before such a criterion can be used with confidence as a chronological tool it is necessary to know exactly its origin. Its formation is so slow that in Egypt, for example, it is estimated that a light brown coating requires between 2,000 and 5,000 years to develop, a fully formed black veneer between 20,000 and 50,000 years. The development of relatively opaque soil horizons that are subsequently exposed at the surface due to erosion of materials that once lay, easily eroded, and which thus become surface crusts, is common in arid areas, although it is also known outside deserts, and indeed many of the examples in arid lands probably originate from earlier periods of humid climates. The crust prevents occasional rainwater from penetrating deep into the soil, thus contributing to the rapid runoff associated with desert storms. premise: When the topic is global warming, the villain is usually America. Although it produces a quarter of the greenhouse gases that warm the planet, it refuses to regulate them. When other countries agreed on an international treaty to do so, the Kyoto Protocol America failed to ratify it. But not all American authorities are satisfied with the position of the federal government. In fact, 12 states disagree so strongly that they are suing to force it to curb emissions of carbon dioxide, the most common greenhouse gas. The Supreme Court heard a plea in the case on November 29. The outcome will not be known for months, but the political spirit appears to be shifting in favour of firmer action against climate change. The Clean Air Act requires the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in regulating air pollution from vehicles. But the EPA argues that Congress did not intend to include CO2 under this heading, and that doing so would expand the EPA's authority to an unreasonable extent. Moreover, it argues that regulating emissions would do no good unless all other countries or most other countries did the same. This is in line with the policies of President George W. Bush, who opposes mandatory restrictions on emissions and believes any international agreement on global warming should apply to all countries opposed to the Kyoto Protocol, which exempts poor, including major polluters like China and India. Ten states, including gas-drinking Texas and car-making Michigan, also support the EPA. The plaintiffs include 12 countries, three cities, various NGOs and American Samoa, a Pacific territory in danger of disappearing beneath the rising ocean. They are supported by six other states, two electricity companies, a ski resort, and diverse clergy, Indian tribes and agitated bigwigs like Madeleine Albright, the former secretary of state. They point out that under the direction of Bill Clinton, the EPA decided it had the authority to regulate CO2. The law, they note, says that the EPA should regulate any air pollutant that might reasonably be interpreted to endanger public health or the public welfare\. It goes on to define public welfare to include\ impacts on soils, water, crops, vegetation, man-made materials, animals, wildlife, weather, visibility and climate\. The Supreme Court might give a mixed ruling, ruling that carbon dioxide is indeed a pollutant, but one that the EPA is free to ignore or regulate at will. Or she may reject the complaint on the grounds that the plaintiffs had no right to file it in the first place. In theory, they must prove that the EPA's foot ambassador caused them specific harm that regulation might fix a tall order in a field fraught with uncertainties like climate. Even if the court finds in favor of the plaintiffs, quick change is unlikely. By the time the EPA implemented such a ruling, Congress probably would have replaced it with a new law. That's the point, say environmental groups. They want Congress to pass a law tackling global warming, and hope a favorable court ruling will please politicians. Moreover, the case has an impact on a number of other bitterly disputed lawsuits. Automakers, for example, are trying to get the courts to overturn a California state law based on certain provisions of the Clean Air Act that require them to reduce the CO2 emissions of their vehicles. If the Supreme Court decides the act doesn't apply to CO2, then California law would be in jeopardy, too. This, in turn, would hurt the decision of ten other countries to adopt the same standard. However, the Supreme Court states, many countries' governments are determined to tackle climate change. California is in the vanguard. Its legislature passed a law that would cover and then reduce industrial emissions of greenhouse gases. Seven eastern states have set up the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, which will treat emissions from power plants the same way. Nearly 400 mayors have signed an agreement to cut their cities' emissions in accordance with Kyoto. Many businesses, even some electricity companies, would rather see regulation now than prolonged uncertainty. And some of the leading contenders for the 2008 presidential election are far more inclined to emissions limits than Bush. Change is in the air.
hypothesis: An American island is in danger of disappearing beneath the rising ocean.

premise: Walking on water and the availability of groundwater has always been taken for granted by Australians. GROUNDWATER SUPPLY WAS SEEN IN PREVIOUS ERAS AS A RESOURCE OF INFINITE LIMITS, THE PROFIT MINDSET WAS OUT OF SIGHT. All this has changed with modern times. Persistent neglect has resulted in many complications for groundwater users and many interest groups have a large part in its management and allocation. Over-allocation of surface water and ongoing water scarcity mean that reliance on groundwater supplies is likely to swell. The main point of concern now is whether or not a groundwater source can provide a sustainable yield. This relies on proper management of discharge (outflow) and loading (flow) rates. Discharge occurs when humans eject water as well as through vegetation and evaporation into the atmosphere. Sustainable use therefore depends on more than maintaining the rate of recharge: if humans use water exactly at the rate of recharge, discharging in other ways could be adversely affected. Queensland has been one of the most active states in managing groundwater supplies. This is because the territory sits atop the Great Artesian Basin (GAB) an extensive undersea aquifer that covers nearly a fifth of mainland Australia. This resource has long been used by indigenous people and outback communities, especially during periods of drought (when surface water may dry up for hundreds of miles at the edge). Since farmers in the Caribbean pioneered the use of hatcheries in the country, the number has risen beyond sustainable levels causing a decrease in water pressure and flow rate across the region. Furthermore, estimates suggest that 80% of GAB exports are wasted because of inefficient and outdated supply systems. Open drains used to retain livestock moisture are a particular blow and many water is lost due to seepage and evaporation. A number of initiatives have been taken to help eliminate this problem. THE QUEENSLAND GOVERNMENT ANNOUNCED IN 2005 A FREEZE ON THE ISSUANCE OF NEW LICENCES TO EXTRACT WATER FROM THE GAB. A strategy group known as the Great Artesian Basin Advisory Council also released a management plan that included capping some holes (to prevent further drops in pressure) and restoring hundreds of other holes and draining drilling with troughs and polyester piping (to prevent water seeping into the ground). It is now also evident that the corruption of groundwater supply by humans is going to be an issue to be tackled. In 2006, thousands of Sydney residents had their groundwater use reduced due to industrial pollution of the Botany Stalls aquifer. Drilling water for any domestic purpose has since been off-limits due to chemical seepage from about 8 industrial sites. However, groundwater programs are continuing apace. Development of a controversial desalination facility has been postponed indefinitely while the feasibility of exploiting two aquifers near Sydney is investigated. Authorities intend to use aquifers to provide up to 30 giglitres of water a year during dry periods and then leave them alone to regenerate during years of higher rainfall. But the proposed plan is laden with difficulties: Low flow rates hamper extraction: replenishment rates are lower than expected, and salinity imbalances caused by the procedure could wreak havoc in efforts to preserve wetland vegetation and animal ecosystems that rely on abundant, clean and steady supplies of water from aquifers. It's not too late to turn groundwater into a sustainable resource. Groundwater is replenished via surface flow (and at a much slower rate, in organic springs where it is literally drip-fed through rock on its way to aquifers). Currently, however, experts believe excessive amounts of groundwater are being wasted on aesthetic projects such as maintaining parks, gardens and green golf courses. Besides more judicious use of groundwater, many experts believe that we must examine harnessing other potential sources in order to meet our water needs. During rainy seasons, for example, urban areas are flooded with storm water and flash floods that can bring cities to a standstill. Better storm water control mechanisms may capture and retain this rainwater for use at a later date.
hypothesis: Australians have always regarded groundwater as a precious resource.

premise: Water and chips are breaking new ground Computers have been shrinking since their conception nearly two centuries ago, and the trend should continue with recent developments in microchip manufacturing. The earliest prototype of a mechanical computer was called the Difference Engine, and was invented by an eccentric Victorian named Charles Babbage. Its weight was over 15 tons and had 26,000 parts. Colossus, the first electronic computer, did not appear until the end of WWTI, and with its 1,500 vacuum tubes was even more complex and much heavier than its mechanical predecessor. It was only when the silicon-based microchip was invented in the early 1950s that computers began to become more compact. The first microchip computers were very complex and had more than 100,000 transistors, or electronic switches; however, they were still quite bulky and measured several feet wide. Today microchips are measured in nanometers (nanometers) meaning in billions of meters and the search for even smaller chips continues as scientists work on new methods to make chips. Today, most microchips are shaped by a process called lithographic etching, which uses ultraviolet (UV) light. A beam of UV light with a wavelength of only 193 nm is projected through a lens onto an etching mask, a micro-device with long narrow slits or cuts. When UV light hits the surface of the silicon chips, it removes microscopic layers of silicon to create patterns for the microchip circuitry. Chips with features as small as 65 nm can be created with this wavelength. However, lithographic etching is not capable of producing chips much smaller than 65 nm because of the fundamental properties of light. If the slit in the mask were made narrower, the air and nitrogen used in the space between the lens and the etching mask would scatter the light and cause a blurry image. This means that 193 nm UV light cannot be used to make chips with features smaller than 65 nm. Manufacturers know that they need to be even smaller for the technological demands of this century, and they are looking for new methods to make chips. One approach to solving the problem is to use microscopic mirrors to focus X-rays rather than ultraviolet light. X-rays can be generated at wavelengths of less than 25 nm, allowing engineers to produce components smaller than 15 nm. The process is known as X-ray lithography etching. However, this technology is extremely expensive, so manufacturers continue to look for a cheaper alternative. A technology called immersion lithography may be the solution. Although liquids aren't typically associated with computers, a tiny drop of water may be all it takes to make processors smaller and more powerful. Intel and IBM, who created the first microprocessors, have recently developed a unique method for making chips, which uses drops of water to allow manufacturers to shrink the chips at an affordable price! The new microchip is manufactured using a drop of water to narrow the gap between the light source and the etching mask, and shorten the wavelength of UV light to less than 34 nanometers. This process can be used to produce chips as small as 45 nm, or possibly even smaller. Initially, engineers feared air vents and other contaminants in water droplets would distort the light and ruin the microchip etching process, and the first experiments proved that these concerns were well-founded. The problem was overcome by the use of high-purity water, without air and other substances. Scientists are also experimenting with water-dense non-liquid liquids such as hydrofluoric acid that may allow the wavelength to shrink even further, thus producing even smaller chips. IBM has already successfully implemented immersion lithography in some of its production lines and created a fully functional processor. IBM also claims that they are capable of producing chips with very few flaws. Although immersion lithography is very new, it is very promising because it will make the production of 45nm and 32nm chips commercially viable. This is a significant milestone in chip manufacturing and will help lower chip costs without fundamentally altering microchip manufacturing processes. In the near future, the groundbreaking technology of immersion lithography will allow computer manufacturers to produce powerful chips that will be used in electronic devices smaller than a coin. This will open up new opportunities in the ever-shrinking world of digital technology.
hypothesis: The first electronic computer weighed more than the first mechanical prototype.
