premise: Water pressure and water shortage Pressure and water scarcity occur when there is an imbalance between water availability and water demand. When we hear people talk about water pressure and scarcity, we often think of drought, but this is only one of several reasons. Alex Karpov, WHO representative explains some of the other issues that also affect the availability of fresh water, the deterioration of groundwater and surface water quality, the competition for water between different sectors of society, for example, between agricultural, industrial and household users, and even social and economic barriers, they all cause stress and scarcity of water today. While three-quarters of the Earth is covered with water, only a small fraction of it is available as fresh water. Of the available freshwater supply, nearly 70% is withdrawn and used for irrigation for food production, and demand just keeps growing. Although there is currently no global water shortage, more and more regions of the world are suffering from chronic water shortages. Currently, 1.1 billion people have no choice but to use potentially harmful water sources, and 2.6 billion people, which is about half of the developing world, lack access to adequate sanitation. As Kathy Coles, director of the charity Waterworld, describes, the situation will deteriorate. Over the next 20 years, an estimated 1.8 billion people will live in countries or regions with a complete lack of water, and two-thirds of the world's population may be under stress conditions. This situation will only get worse, as fast-growing urban areas put heavy pressure on the water supply. Of course, there have been various initiatives set up around the world to help with water stress and shortages. With larger scale projects, like the construction of Piper Water Systems, remaining important goals of many development agencies, a shortage of time and funds will leave hundreds of millions of people without access to safe water for the foreseeable future. Georgina Ronaldson, a spokeswoman for the World Bank, recently announced a way to deal with the current difficulties. To help developing countries, various concerned organizations have developed the Safe Water System (SWS), which is an adaptable and flexible intervention that uses scientific methods appropriate to the developing world. SWS has been criticised in various corners as too amateurish, yet Ronaldson continues to justify the approach. The use of relevant technologies is important, and in many places around the world water supply efforts suffer from a lack of technical knowledge to effectively manage or adapt a system to the changing needs of the community. The SWS is a community-based integrative approach to improving health and quality of life through an increased approach to improving water, sanitation and hygiene. Darren Stanford, a water quality engineer, explains the crucial methodology in three steps. The first is the evaluation of the water supply system from the basin to the consumer. The second is the implementation of appropriate interventions, which can include protection of source water, improvements in water supply systems, introduction of SWS, sanitation improvement and hygiene education. The third is assessing the impact of the intervention of the health and quality of life of consumers. One example of how poor access to water can affect local populations is the problems of guinea worms in remote areas of Africa. It is a preventable parasitic infection that afflicts poor communities that lack safe drinking water. The infection is transmitted to people who drink water containing copepods (tiny water fleas) infected with larvae of guinea worms. After ingestion, these larvae take up to a year to grow into adult worms; the female worms then emerge from the skin anywhere in the body. Will Goodman, a doctor at the WHO, says it can affect communities in different ways. The emergence of the adult worm can be very painful, slow and embarrassing and prevents people from working in their fields, caring for their animals, going to school and caring for their families. Today many organizations are helping the last nine endemic countries (all in sub-Saharan Africa) eradicate Guinea worm. SINCE THE GUINEA WORM CONTROL PROGRAM BEGAN, GUINEA WORM INCIDENCE HAS DECLINED FROM 1.5 MILLION CASES PER YEAR IN 20 ENDEMIC COUNTRIES TO 25,018 CASES REPORTED IN 2008 FROM THE NINE REMAINING ENDEMIC COUNTRIES. Eradication efforts make use of simple intervention to supply safe drinking water, including using cloth filters and hose filters to filter the infected copods from water, applying chemicals to the water supply to kill the larvae, and preventing infected individuals from entering and contaminating the water supply, as the worms emerge from their mouths. The supply of drilling wells and other water supply in the endemic village is another important component of the eradication efforts. Drilling well supply is one of the main objectives of SWS. Many wells dug in settlements penetrate only the topsoil, do not reach sufficient depth and are therefore easily affected by drought or the natural declines from summer to autumn in the water table. SWS drilling wells can penetrate the rock and access a deeper aquifer with water unaffected by surface drought. These are also unaffected by the spread of guinea worms and water is much safer for human consumption.
hypothesis: Most of the water that exists on Earth is drinkable.

Alex Karpov, WHO representative explains some of the other issues that also affect the availability of fresh water, the deterioration of groundwater and surface water quality, the competition for water between different sectors of society, for example, between agricultural, industrial and household users, and even social and economic barriers, they all cause stress and scarcity of water today. While three-quarters of the Earth is covered with water, only a small fraction of it is available as fresh water. Of the available freshwater supply, nearly 70% is withdrawn and used for irrigation for food production, and demand just keeps growing. Although there is currently no global water shortage, more and more regions of the world are suffering from chronic water shortages. Currently, 1.1 billion people have no choice but to use potentially harmful water sources, and 2.6 billion people, which is about half of the developing world, lack access to adequate sanitation. As Kathy Coles, director of the charity Waterworld, describes, the situation will deteriorate. Over the next 20 years, an estimated 1.8 billion people will live in countries or regions with a complete lack of water, and two-thirds of the world's population may be under stress conditions. This situation will only get worse, as fast-growing urban areas put heavy pressure on the water supply. Of course, there have been various initiatives set up around the world to help with water stress and shortages. With larger scale projects, like the construction of Piper Water Systems, remaining important goals of many development agencies, a shortage of time and funds will leave hundreds of millions of people without access to safe water for the foreseeable future. Georgina Ronaldson, a spokeswoman for the World Bank, recently announced a way to deal with the current difficulties. To help developing countries, various concerned organizations have developed the Safe Water System (SWS), which is an adaptable and flexible intervention that uses scientific methods appropriate to the developing world. SWS has been criticised in various corners as too amateurish, yet Ronaldson continues to justify the approach. The use of relevant technologies is important, and in many places around the world water supply efforts suffer from a lack of technical knowledge to effectively manage or adapt a system to the changing needs of the community. The SWS is a community-based integrative approach to improving health and quality of life through an increased approach to improving water, sanitation and hygiene. Darren Stanford, a water quality engineer, explains the crucial methodology in three steps. The first is the evaluation of the water supply system from the basin to the consumer. The second is the implementation of appropriate interventions, which can include protection of source water, improvements in water supply systems, introduction of SWS, sanitation improvement and hygiene education. The third is assessing the impact of the intervention of the health and quality of life of consumers. One example of how poor access to water can affect local populations is the problems of guinea worms in remote areas of Africa. It is a preventable parasitic infection that afflicts poor communities that lack safe drinking water. The infection is transmitted to people who drink water containing copepods (tiny water fleas) infected with larvae of guinea worms. After ingestion, these larvae take up to a year to grow into adult worms; the female worms then emerge from the skin anywhere in the body. Will Goodman, a doctor at the WHO, says it can affect communities in different ways. The emergence of the adult worm can be very painful, slow and embarrassing and prevents people from working in their fields, caring for their animals, going to school and caring for their families. Today many organizations are helping the last nine endemic countries (all in sub-Saharan Africa) eradicate Guinea worm. SINCE THE GUINEA WORM CONTROL PROGRAM BEGAN, GUINEA WORM INCIDENCE HAS DECLINED FROM 1.5 MILLION CASES PER YEAR IN 20 ENDEMIC COUNTRIES TO 25,018 CASES REPORTED IN 2008 FROM THE NINE REMAINING ENDEMIC COUNTRIES. Eradication efforts make use of simple intervention to supply safe drinking water, including using cloth filters and hose filters to filter the infected copods from water, applying chemicals to the water supply to kill the larvae, and preventing infected individuals from entering and contaminating the water supply, as the worms emerge from their mouths. The supply of drilling wells and other water supply in the endemic village is another important component of the eradication efforts. Drilling well supply is one of the main objectives of SWS. Many wells dug in settlements penetrate only the topsoil, do not reach sufficient depth and are therefore easily affected by drought or the natural declines from summer to autumn in the water table. SWS drilling wells can penetrate the rock and access a deeper aquifer with water unaffected by surface drought. These are also unaffected by the spread of guinea worms and water is much safer for human consumption.

premise: Waterfalls cascades are places where rivers or streams direct their flow on vertical drops. They have always been a temptation for their scenic beauty or, in the case of the greatest, for their ability to display the power and majesty of nature. Niagara Falls, on the border of Canada and America (which produces the most water of all), is a stone draw for visitors, as does Victoria Falls, which also lie on an international border between Zimbabwe and Zambia, and feature the largest falling water sheet in the world. Similarly, the remoteness and inaccessibility of the highest waterfall, Angel Falls, located deep in the middle of the Venezuelan jungle, has not prevented it from becoming one of the country's top tourist attractions. There are many possible causes for waterfalls, but one common one is differences in rock type. When a river flows over a resistant rock substrate, erosion is slow, but with the complex geological faulting of the earth's surface, softer rock patches can be exposed. The water cuts into this, resulting in slight turbulence at the boundary, and giving rise to pebbles and gravel from the river embankment, which increases the erosion capacity of the stream. And so begins a process in which the river gets two layers, or levels, and a waterfall is born. Other sudden causes of falls are earthquakes or landslides, which create fault lines on land, or divert waterways, respectively. In addition, in recent ice ages, glaciers scoured many deep basins. These glaciers may have disappeared, but their feeder rivers can continue to flow as waterfalls into the remaining depressions. Obviously then, waterfalls come in a variety of shapes and sizes, as different as the local geology in which they are found, and this has resulted in an abundance of descriptive terms. The word cataract simply refers to a large and powerful waterfall, while a waterfall descends in a series of rock steps. If these steps differ greatly, it is a cascading waterfall, and if each step is even larger, about the same size, and with a substantial pool of water at each base, it is known as a multi-stage waterfall. IF THE FALLING WATER ENGAGES THE ROCK FACE, IT OFTEN EXPANDS, TO BE CALLED A HORSETAIL WATERFALL, WHILE IF IT DOES NOT TOUCH THE ROCK FACE AT ALL, IT IS A DIVING WATERFALL FOR MOST OFTEN THE MOST PICTURESQUE. Regardless of such differences, all waterfalls have in common a vertical height and an average water flow. These properties, taken together, are a measure of the force of the falls, quantified using a ten-point logarithmic scale. Giant waterfalls, such as Niagara, are ranked at the top of this scale, finding smaller waterfalls, which may occur in the city's streams, at the bottom. Another common feature of larger waterfalls is a deep-water pool. This is caused by the debris at the base of the falls, which mixes and breaks into smaller pieces. In the never-ending swirls and swirls, these pieces scour a deep underwater basin. An interesting result is that such falls are in the process of retraction, since the softer material in the lower face suffers from undercutting. THIS GIVES RISE TO SHELTERS FOR ROCKS BEHIND THE FALLING WATER, WHICH BECOME STEADILY LARGER UNTIL THE ROOF COLLAPSES, AND THE WATERFALL RECEDES SIGNIFICANTLY BACK TO EARTH. Of course, to people in general, a waterfall seems permanent and forever. Erosion is indeed a slow process; however, given a sufficiently strong waterfall and the right type of rock, the retreat can be over a metre per year. This will be clearly visible throughout human life, and a fast-moving display, spanning several decades, will show a fundamentally unchanged height of falling water settling back in surprising uniformity. Because this movement is towards higher elevations or through more mountainous terrain, a series of geological features can be assumed in the path of the retreat of the falls. Victoria Falls is an excellent example, with its lower parts being characterised by spectacular islands, gorges and rock formations. This retreat occasionally causes problems, as seen in Niagara Falls. In just over ten millennia, the falls have moved nearly 11 miles upstream. Because the Niagara River marks the Canada—America border, as agreed in 1819, the identifiable retreat of these waterfalls since that time technically means that the Canadian border has moved forward at the expense of America, though it is clear that this argument has caused controversy. More practically, with so much infrastructure, like hotels, roads, bridges and scenic vantage points, all rigidly established, it remains important to limit erosion. FOR THIS REASON, THE EXPOSED WATERFALL RIDGES WERE EXTENSIVELY STRENGTHENED, AND UNDERWATER BARRIERS WERE INSTALLED TO DIVERT THE MORE EROSIVE RIVER CURRENTS. The most ambitious erosion control measure occurred in 1969 at the American Niagara Falls, whose retreat lay in American territory. The branch of the Niagara River feeding these daughter waterfalls was closed, allowing the main Horseshoe Falls to absorb the excess flow. The then dry and exposed riverbed and cliff face allowed a team of US Army engineers to use screws, cement and brackets, to reinforce any unstable rock. Five months later, the temporary dam was destroyed with explosives, returning water to the falls, but the inevitable erosion process slowed considerably.

premise: What do managers really do? When students graduate and first enter the workforce, the most common choice is to find an entry-level position. This can be a job such as an unpaid internship, assistant, secretary or junior associate position. Traditionally, we start with simpler jobs and work our way up. Young professionals begin the program to become senior partners, associates or even managers of a workplace. However, these promotions can be few and far between, leaving many young professionals unfamiliar with management experience. An important step is understanding the role and responsibility of a person in a managerial role. Managers are members of an organization responsible for the work performance of other members of the organization. Managers have formal authority to use organizational resources and make decisions. Managers at different levels of the organization are engaged in different periods of time in the four administrative functions of planning, organizing, transporting and controlling. However, as many professionals already know, style management can be very different depending on where you work. Some management styles are strictly hierarchical. Other management styles can be more casual and relaxed, with the manager likely to behave more like a team member rather than a strict boss. Many researchers have created a more scientific approach in studying these different approaches to management. In the 1960s, researcher Henry Mintzberg created a constitutive organizational model using three categories. These categories represent three main functional approaches, which are designated aspersonal, informative, and decisive. Introduced Category 1: Interpersonal Roles. Interpersonal roles require managers to direct and supervise employees and the organization. The head of the figure is usually an interim senior executive. This manager may convey future organizational goals or ethical guidelines to employees at company meetings. They also participate in ribbon-cutting ceremonies, host receptions, presentations, and other activities related to the role of the character. A leader serves as an example for other employees to follow, gives orders and instructions to subordinates, makes decisions, and enlists employee support. They are also responsible for the selection and training of employees. Managers must be leaders at all levels of the organization; often lower-level managers look to senior management for this example of leadership. In the role of liaison, a manager must coordinate the work of others in different work units, establish alliances between others and work to share resources. This role is especially critical for interim managers, who often must compete with other managers for important resources, but must maintain a successful working relationship with them for long periods of time. Category 2 presented: Information roles. Information roles are those in which managers obtain and transmit information. These roles have changed dramatically as technology has improved. The monitor evaluates the performance of others and takes corrective action to improve that performance. Monitors also observe changes in the environment and within the company that may affect personal and organizational performance. Monitoring takes place at all levels of management. The role of the distributor requires managers to inform employees about changes that affect them and the organization. They also convey the vision and purpose of the company. Introduced Category 3: Decision Roles. Decision roles require managers to plan strategy and utilize resources. There are four specific roles that are indispensable. The role of the entrepreneur requires the manager to allocate resources for the development of innovative products and services, or to expand a business. The Disorder Therapist corrects unforeseen problems faced by the organization from the internal or external environment. The third decision role, that of a resource allocator, includes determining which units of work will receive which resources. Senior managers may make large and overall budgetary decisions, while interim managers may make more specific assignments. Finally, the negotiator works with others, such as suppliers, distributors or labor unions, to reach agreements about products and services. Although Mintzberg's initial research in the 1960s helped classify executive approaches, Mintzberg was still concerned about research involving other workplace roles. Mintzberg considered expanding his research into other roles, such as the role of distributor, character, link, and speaker. The study, when applied to real-life situations, did not always improve the actual management process in real life. premise: What you need to know about culture shock Most people who move to a foreign country or culture may experience a period of time where they feel very homesick and have a lot of stress and difficulty functioning in the new culture. This feeling is often called culture shock and it is important to understand and learn how to deal with culture shock if you want to successfully adapt to the culture of your new homes. First of all, it is important to know that culture shock is normal. Anyone in a new situation will go through some kind of culture shock, and its extent is determined by factors such as the difference between cultures, the degree to which someone is anxious to adapt to a new culture and the familiarity a person has to the new culture. If you go, for example, to a vastly different culture than your own, you're likely to experience culture shock more sharply than those who move to a new culture knowing the language and behavioral norms of the new culture. There are four general stages of cultural adaptation, and it is important that you are aware of these stages and be able to recognize what stage you are in and when, so that you understand why you feel the way you do and that all the difficulties you experience are temporary, a process that you are going through and not a permanent situation. The first phase is commonly referred to as the excitement phase or honeymoon phase. Upon arrival in a new environment, you will be interested in the new culture, everything will look exciting, everyone will look friendly and helpful and you will be flooded with impressions. At this point you are simply absorbing the new landscape, passively picking up these impressions, at which point you have little meaningful experience of the culture. But it's not long before the honeymoon phase dissolves into the second phase sometimes called the withdrawal phase. The excitement you felt before turns into frustration because you find it difficult to cope with the problems that arise. It seems that everything is difficult, it is difficult to learn the language, unusual and unpredictable people, friends are difficult to make, and simple things like shopping and going to the bank are challenges. At this point, you're likely to feel anxious and homesick, and you'll probably find yourself complaining about the new culture or country. This is the stage known as culture shock. Culture shock is only temporary, and at some point, if you are one of those who manage to stem it, you will move into the third stage of cultural adaptation, the stage of recovery. At this point, you will have a routine, and you will feel more confident in functioning in the new culture. You'll start to feel less isolated as you start to understand and accept the way things are done and the way people behave in your new environment. Customs and traditions are clearer and easier to understand. At this point, you will face new challenges with humor rather than anxiety. The last stage is the home or stability phase This is the point at which people begin to feel at home in the new culture. At this point, you will function well in the new culture, adopt certain traits and behaviors from your new home, and prefer certain aspects of the new culture over your culture. There is, in a sense, a fifth stage in this process. If you decide to return home after a long stint in a new culture, you may experience what's called reverse culture shock. This means that you may find aspects of your culture foreign because you are so used to the new culture that you have spent so much time adjusting to it. Reverse culture shock is usually pretty mild, you may notice things in your home culture that you've never noticed before, and some of the ways people do things may seem strange. Reverse culture shock rarely lasts very long.
hypothesis: Some people will find the process of adapting to a new country easier than others.

premise: What is the purpose of gaining knowledge? “I would set up an institution where every person could find instruction in any subject.” This was the motto of the founder of Cornell University, and seems to be an apt characterization of the different university, also in the US, where I now teach philosophy. A student can prepare for a career in resort management, engineering, interior design, accounting, music, law enforcement, you name it. But what would the founders of these two institutions have thought of a course called Ignition for Profit? I'm not kidding you: we have it in the books. Any undergraduate who has met the academic requirements can enroll in a course in our program in Fire Science. Naturally, the course is designed for potential arson investigators, who can learn all the tricks of the trade to find out whether a fire was started deliberately, find out who did it, and establish a chain of evidence for effective prosecution in a court of law. But wouldn't it also be the perfect course for potential lighters to sign up to? My point is not to criticise academic programmes in fire science: they are welcomed as part of the increasing professionalisation of many other occupations. However, it is not known that a firefighter would set fire to a building. This example suggests how dishonest and illegal behavior, with the help of higher education, can sneak into every aspect of public and business life. I REREALIZED THIS WHEN I WAS INVITED TO SPEAK BEFORE A CLASS IN MARKETING, WHICH IS ANOTHER OF OUR DEGREE PROGRAMS. The regular instructor is a colleague who appreciates the kind of ethical perspective I can bring as a philosopher. There are endless ways I could have approached this task, but I took my cue from the course title: 'Principles of Marketing'. It made me think to ask the students, 'Is marketing a principle? 'After all, a subject can have principles in the sense of codification, which has rules, as in football or chess, without being principled in the sense of being ethical. Many of the students immediately assumed that the answer to my question about the principles of marketing was obvious: no. Just look at the ways in which anything under the sun is marketed; obviously it shouldn't be done in a principled (=ethical) way. Is it obvious? I made the suggestion, which may sound insane in light of the evidence, that perhaps marketing is by definition principled. My inspiration for this judgment is the philosopher Immanuel Kant, who argued that every body of knowledge consists of a goal (or purpose) and a means. Let us apply both the terms' interpretation 'and' end 'to marketing. Students enrolled in the course in order to learn how to market effectively. But for what purpose? There seem to be two main positions to this question. One is that the answer is obvious: the goal of marketing is to sell things and make money. The other approach is that the goal of marketing is irrelevant: each person comes to the program and course with his own plans, and these do not even have to engage in the acquisition of marketing expertise as such. My suggestion, which I think would also be Kant's, is that none of these approaches grasp the meaning of purpose for the marketing means. A field of knowledge or professional endeavor is defined both by the means and by the objective; hence both deserve scrutiny. Students need to learn both how to achieve X, and also what X. At this point 'ignition for profit' becomes extremely relevant. Apparently this course deals with the means: how to detect and prosecute criminal activity. It is therefore assumed that the ending is good in the ethical sense. WHEN I ASK FIRE SCIENCE STUDENTS TO FORMULATE THE END, OR GOAL, OF THEIR FIELD, THEY END UP GENERALIZING TO SOMETHING LIKE, 'THE SAFETY AND WELFARE OF SOCIETY', WHICH SEEMS TO BE TRUE. As we have seen, someone can use the same knowledge of means to achieve a much less noble goal, such as personal gain through destructive, dangerous and reckless activity. But we wouldn't call it firefighting. We have a separate word for it: arson. Similarly, if you used 'marketing principles' in a non-principled way, you wouldn't be doing marketing. We have another term for it: fraud. Kant gives an example of a doctor and a poisoner, who use the same knowledge to achieve their different goals. We'd say one deals with medicine, the other, murder.
hypothesis: The 'ignition for profit' course will be useful for people who intend to set fire to buildings.

premise: What's in the blood? Blood is the most special fluid in living animals, and plays an absolutely critical role. It symbolizes life (new blood), health (your blood flow), personality (good or bad blood), and family (your bloodline). This red liquid itself is something that most people prefer not to see, and yet it contains such a complex soup of proteins, sugars, ions, hormones, gases and basic cellular components that it is definitely worth considering in some detail. By volume, half of the blood is the liquid part, called plasma. The rest is made up of special components, the main one being red blood cells (technically known as erythrocytes). These transport oxygen molecules throughout the body, and also give the blood its color (from the hemoglobin protein inside it, which turns red when combined with oxygen). Red blood cells, like all cells in the human body, have a limited operating life. They are produced within the bone marrow, mostly the larger ones, and live for about four months before falling inactive, then reabsorbed by the spleen and liver, when the waste products are absorbed in the urine. It contrasts with the other main cells of human blood: the white blood cells, which are technically called leukocytes. They are produced in a similar way in the bone marrow, they are only active for three or four days, but they are essential for protecting the body from infections. White blood cells come in many different types, each designed to counter a different type of invading bacteria, virus, fungus, or parasite. When one of these enters the body, white blood cells quickly determine its character, and then, having recruited a sufficient number of a particular type (the period when you are sick), they launch themselves into the fight, enveloping each individual invasive cell and breaking it down (which leads to recovery). This leaves the last major component of blood: platelets. Their technical name is thrombocytes, and they are much smaller than red and white blood cells. Also freely circulating, they are responsible for blood clotting, which is necessary to heal both external and internal injuries. Again, they are produced in the bone marrow, and have the interesting ability to transform. There are several diseases associated with a breakdown in the regulation of their number. If too low, excessive bleeding can occur, but if too high, internal clotting can form, causing catastrophic blockages in body parts and medical diseases that we know as strokes, heart attacks and embolisms. The blood complex presents special difficulties in the emergence of emergency transfusions. These are avoided if possible in order to lower the risk of reactions due to blood incompatibility. Unexpected antigens can trigger antibodies to attack blood components, with potentially fatal results. Thus, if transfusions are to be performed, knowledge and a thorough classification of the blood are essential, but with 30 recognized systems in blood groups, containing hundreds of antigens, this poses quite a challenge. The ABO system is the most important. On top of this is the rhesus factor, which is not as simple as positive or negative (as most people think), but includes dozens of antigens. However, they can be grouped into groups that cause similar reactions, forming a certain order. Of course, the simplest system for preventing adverse transfusion reactions is for patients to receive their own blood, for example, in a series of blood donations in preparation for surgery planned a few months in advance. The second-best system is to perform cross-matching, which involves simply mixing samples of patients' blood with the donors, and then microscopic examination for non-formation and a key sign of incompatibility. premise: What is the purpose of gaining knowledge? I would find an institution where every person could find instruction in any subject that was the founding motto of Cornell University, and it seems to be an apt characterization of the various university, also in the US, where I currently teach philosophy. A student can prepare for a career in resort management, engineering, interior design, accounting, music, law enforcement, you name it. But what would the founders of these two institutions have thought of a course called Ignition for Profit? I'm not kidding you: we have it in the books. Any undergraduate who has met the academic requirements can enroll in a course in our Fire Science program. Naturally, the course is designed for potential arson investigators, who can learn all the tricks of the trade to find out whether a fire was started deliberately, find out who did it, and establish a chain of evidence for effective prosecution in a court of law. But wouldn't it also be the perfect course for potential lighters to sign up to? My point is not to criticise academic programmes in fire science: they are welcomed as part of the increasing professionalisation of many other occupations. However, it is not known for a firefighter to burn down a building. This example suggests how dishonest and illegal behavior, with the help of higher education, can sneak into every aspect of public and business life. I REREALIZED THIS WHEN I WAS INVITED TO SPEAK BEFORE A CLASS IN MARKETING, WHICH IS ANOTHER OF OUR DEGREE PROGRAMS. The regular instructor is a colleague who appreciates the kind of ethical perspective I can bring as a philosopher. There are endless ways I could have approached this task, but I took my cue from the course title: Principles of Marketing. It made me think to ask the students, is marketing principled? After all, a subject can have principles in the sense of codification, rules, as in football or chess, without being principled in the sense of being ethical. Many of the students immediately assumed that the answer to my question about the principles of marketing was obvious: no. Just look at the ways in which anything under the sun is marketed; obviously it shouldn't be done in a principled (=ethical) way. Is it obvious? I made the suggestion, which may sound insane in light of the evidence, that perhaps marketing is by definition principled. My inspiration for this judgment is the philosopher Immanuel Kant, who argued that every body of knowledge consists of a goal (or purpose) and a means. Let us apply both the terms “means” and the ending to marketing. Students enrolled in the course in order to learn how to market effectively. But for what purpose? There seem to be two main positions to this question. One is that the answer is obvious: the goal of marketing is to sell things and make money. The other approach is that the goal of marketing is irrelevant: each person comes to the program and course with his own plans, and these do not even have to engage in the acquisition of marketing expertise as such. My suggestion, which I think would also be Kants, is that none of these approaches grasp the meaning of purpose for the marketing means. A field of knowledge or professional endeavor is defined both by the means and by the objective; hence both deserve scrutiny. Students need to learn both how to achieve X, and also what X. It is at this point that ignition for profit becomes extremely relevant. Apparently this course deals with the means: how to detect and prosecute criminal activity. It is therefore assumed that the ending is good in the ethical sense. When I ask fire science students to formulate the end, or goal, of their field, they end up generalizing to something like, the safety and welfare of society, which seems to be true. As we have seen, someone can use the same knowledge of means to achieve a much less noble goal, such as personal gain through destructive, dangerous and reckless activity. But we wouldn't call it firefighting. We have a separate word for it: arson. Similarly, if you used the principles of marketing in a non-principled way, you wouldn't be doing marketing. We have another term for it: fraud. Kant gives an example of a doctor and a poisoner, who use the same knowledge to achieve their different goals. We'd say one deals with medicine, the other, murder.

premise: When conversations flow we spend a large part of our daily lives talking to other people and as a result we are very used to the art of conversation. But why do we feel comfortable in conversations that have a flow, but become nervous and funny when a conversation is interrupted by unexpected silences? To answer this question, we will first look at some of the effects of conversation flow. We will then explain how flow can serve different social needs. The positive consequences of call flow show some similarities with the effects of processing flux. Research has shown that flux processing and the ease with which individuals process information affects people's judgments across a wide range of social dimensions. For example, people feel that when something is easily processed, it is more correct or more accurate. Moreover, they have more confidence in their judgments about information that has come to them on a regular basis, and they like things that are easy to process more than things that are difficult to process. Studies indicate that the speaker is considered more knowledgeable when answering questions immediately; responding with non-fluent speech markers like oh or jug or simply staying quiet for a moment too long can destroy this positive image. One of the social needs that relate to the flow of conversation is the human need for synchronization or harmony with each other. Many studies have shown how people try to synchronize with their partners, by coordinating their behavior. This interpersonal coordination underlies a wide range of human activities, from more complicated ones like ballroom dancing to simply walking or chatting with friends. In conversations, interpersonal coordination is found when people adjust the duration of their utterances and the pace of their speech to each other so that they can allow turn-taking to occur, without talking to each other or experiencing awkward silences. Because people are well trained to have conversations, they are often able to switch turns within milliseconds, resulting in a conversation flow of seamlessly networked behaviors. Lack of flow is characterized by interruptions, simultaneous speech or mutual silences. Avoiding these traits is important for defining and maintaining interpersonal relationships. The need to belong has been identified as one of the most basic human motivations and plays a role in many human behaviors. Association-related call flow may be most easily highlighted by the consequences of flow disruptions. What happens when the positive experience of the flow is interrupted, for example, by a brief silence? We all know that silences can be quite embarrassing, and studies show that even brief disruptions to the flow of conversation can lead to a sharp increase in levels of distress. In films, silences are often used to signal disobedience or confrontation (Piazza, 2006). Some researchers even argue that silencing someone is one of the most serious forms of exclusion. Group membership is of fundamental importance to our well-being and because humans are very sensitive to signals of exclusion, silence is usually taken as a sign of rejection. In this way, the lack of flow in the conversation may signal that our relationship is not as solid as we thought it was. Another aspect of synchrony is that people often try to validate their opinions to those of others. That is, people like to see in others similar ideas or worldviews as they have themselves, because this informs people that they are right and their worldviews are justified. The comedian, another superhero in the alternative world of Watchmen, is a thug who hasn't gained a large fan base; his ruthlessness (killing a pregnant Vietnamese woman), the terrifying (attempted rape), psychotic toughness (you only have to look at his panelists shooting for the audience to witness it) is repulsive, not triumphant. This is because the comedian has no purpose: he is a nihilist, and as a nihilist, denies any potential meaning to his friend, and thus to the comic reader. Everything for him is a joke, including his own self, and as a result his own death could be seen as just another argument. Rorschach, on the other hand, believes in something: he asks whether his fight for justice is futile? Then immediately corrects himself, states that there is good and evil, and evil must be punished. Even in the face of Armageddon I won't compromise on that. Jacob Held, in his essay comparing Rorschach's motivation to Kantian ethics, made the assumption that perhaps our dignity lies in behaving as if the world is right, even when it is clear that it is not. Rorschach causes pain in others not because he is a sadist, but because he feels the need to punish injustice and uphold the good, and although he cannot make the world justice, he can act on his sense of righteousness - through the use of violence.

This calculation was widely used by the government of the day to support their immigration policy. The Home Office findings stood out against the findings of other Western countries which found that the benefits of large-scale internal migration are so small that they are close to zero. premise: When evolution goes backwards evolution shouldn't run backwards - but a growing number of examples show that it does and that it can sometimes represent the future of a species. The description of any animal as an evolutionary retreat is controversial. For most of the century, most biologists have shied away from using these words, while being aware of the principle of evolution that says evolution cannot run backwards. But as more and more examples emerge and modern genetics comes into place, this principle must be rewritten. Not only are evolutionary setbacks possible, they sometimes play an important role in the forward march of evolution. THE TECHNICAL TERM FOR EVOLUTIONARY UPHEAVAL IS ATAVISM, FROM THE LATIN ATAEUS, WHICH MEANS ANCESTOR. The word has ugly connotations mainly thanks to Cesare Lombroso, a 19th-century Italian medic who argued that criminals were born uncreated and could be identified by certain physical traits that were throwbacks to a primitive and subhuman condition. While Lombroso was measuring criminals, a Belgian paleontologist named Louis Dulleau researched fossil records and came to the opposite conclusion. In 1890 he proposed that evolution is irreversible: that an organism is incapable of returning, even partially, to a previous stage that had already been realized in the ranks of its ancestors. Biologists in the early 20th century came to a similar conclusion, though they agreed it in terms of probability, stating that there was no reason why evolution couldn't run backwards - it's just very unlikely. AND SO THE IDEA OF IRREVERSIBILITY IN EVOLUTION STALLED AND BECAME KNOWN AS DOLUS'S LAW. If Dolus' law is right, atavisms should occur only very rarely, if ever. Almost since the idea took root, however, exceptions have sprung up. In 1919, for example, a humpback whale with a pair of leg-like appendages more than a meter long, with a full set of limb bones, was caught off Vancouver Island in Canada. Researcher Roy Chapman Andrews argued at the time that the whale must be a throwback to a living ancestor on land. 'I can see no other explanation, 'wrote in 1921. Since then so many other examples have been discovered that it no longer makes sense to say that evolution is as good as irreversible. And this poses a conundrum: how can properties that disappeared millions of years ago suddenly appear? In 1994, Rudolf Raff and colleagues from Indiana University in the US decided to use genetics to put a number on the probability that evolution would reverse. THEY REASONED THAT WHILE SOME EVOLUTIONARY CHANGES INVOLVE THE LOSS OF GENES AND ARE THEREFORE IRREVERSIBLE, OTHERS MAY BE THE RESULT OF GENE SWITCHING OFF. If these silent genes are somehow reactivated, they argued, long-lost traits might reappear. The Reps team went on to calculate the likelihood of that happening. Silent genes accumulate random mutations, they languish, and eventually render them useless. So how long can a gene survive in a species if it is no longer used? The team calculated that there is a good chance that quiet genes will survive up to 6 million years for at least some individuals in the population, and that some may survive for up to 10 million years. In other words, regressions are possible, but only to the relatively recent evolutionary past. As a possible example, the team pointed to the mole salamanders of Mexico and California. Like most amphibians these begin life in a juvenile tadpole state, then undergo metamorphosis into the adult form except for one species, the axolotl, which lives its entire life as a juvenile. The simplest explanation for this is that the Axolotl dynasty alone lost the ability to perform metamorphosis, while others retained it. From a detailed analysis of the salamanders' pedigree, however, it is clear that the other lineages evolved from an ancestor who himself lost the ability to perform metamorphosis. In other words, metamorphosis in mole salamanders is an atavism. The salamander example fits into Raf's time frame of 10 million years.82However, examples breaking the time limit have recently been reported, suggesting that quiet gardens may not be the whole story. In a paper published last year, biologist Gunter Wagner of Yale University reported several works on the evolutionary history of a group of South American lizards called Bachia. Many of them have tiny limbs; some look more like snakes than lizards and few have completely lost their toes on the hind limbs. However, other species include up to four toes on their hind legs. The simplest explanation is that finger lineages never lost their toes, but Wagner begs to differ. premise: When was the last time you saw a frog? Chances are if you live in the city, you haven't seen one in a while. Are amphibians just overly sensitive to ecosystem changes? Could it be that their rapid decline in numbers signals some kind of environmental catastrophe approaching for us all? This frightening scenario is partly the result of a dramatic increase over the past quarter-century in the development of natural areas that were once wet marshes; home not just to frogs but to all kinds of wildlife. However, so far, there are no obvious reasons why certain frog species are disappearing from Australia's rainforests that have barely been touched by a human hand. The mystery is troubling to say the least, since amphibian species are known to be extremely sensitive to environmental changes in temperature and humidity levels. The danger is that the planet may not only lose a vital link in the ecological food chain (frogs maintain populations of otherwise harmful insects at manageable levels), but that we may increase our air pollutant output to levels that may already have become irreversible. Frogs can inadvertently warn us of catastrophe. An example of a frog species that, as far as is known to be extinct, is the platypus frog. Like the well-known Australian mammal he was named after, he demonstrated very odd behaviour; instead of giving birth to tadpoles in the water, he raised his young inside his abdomen. Discovered in 1981, less than ten years later the frog completely disappeared from the clear waters of the Bulumba Creek near Queensland's Sunshine Coast. One theory that seems to fit the facts concerns the depletion of the ozone layer, a well-documented phenomenon that has led to a sharp increase in ultraviolet radiation levels. The ozone layer is designed to protect Earth from UV rays, but increased radiation may have a greater impact on frog populations than previously believed. Another theory is that temperature increases around the world are upsetting the reproductive cycles of frogs.

However, everyone surely remembers their first kiss, for all its embarrassing or delightful details, and the kiss continues to play a big role in new novels. At least, it happens in some companies. People in Western societies may assume that romantic kissing is a universal human behavior, but a new analysis suggests that less than half of all cultures actually do so. Kisses are also extremely rare in the animal kingdom. So what's really behind this bizarre behavior? If it's useful, why don't all animals do it and so do all humans? Apparently the very fact that most animals don't kiss helps explain why some do. According to a new study on kissing preferences, which examined 168 cultures from around the world, only 46% of cultures kiss in a romantic sense. Previous estimates put the figure at 90%. The new study did not include parents kissing their children, and focused solely on lip-on-lip romantic action between couples. Many hunter-gatherer groups showed no evidence of kissing or a desire to do so. Some even thought it was creepy. According to reports, the Mahinako tribe in Brazil said it was disgusting. Given that hunter-gatherer groups are the closest modern humans have to living the lifestyle of our ancestors, our ancestors may not have kissed either. The study dismisses the belief that romantic kissing is an almost universal human behavior, says lead author William Yankovic of the University of Nevada at Las Vegas. Instead it seems to be a product of Western societies, passed down from generation to generation, he says. There is some historical evidence to back this up. It seems that kissing as we do it today is a fairly recent invention, says Raphael Velodarski of the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom. He searched the records to find evidence of how the kissing had changed. The oldest evidence of kiss-type behavior comes from Indian Sanskrit texts from over 3,500 years ago. Kissing has been described as inhaling one another's soul. In contrast, Egyptian hieroglyphs depict people close to each other instead of pressing their lips to each other. So what's going on here? Is kissing something we do naturally, but have been suppressed by certain cultures? Or is it something modern humans invented? We can find some insight by observing animals. Our closest relatives, chimpanzees and bonobos, do kiss. Primatologist Frans de Waal of Emory University in Atlanta, Georgia, has seen many cases of chimpanzees kissing and hugging after a conflict. For chimpanzees, kissing is a form of reconciliation. It is more common among males than females. In other words, it's not romantic behavior. Their bonobo cousins kiss more often, and they often use tongues while doing so. This is perhaps not surprising, because bonobos are highly sexual creatures. When two people meet, we may shake hands. Bonobos have sex: the so-called bonobo handshake. They also use the species for many other types of bonds. So their kisses aren't very romantic either. These two monkeys are exceptions to the rule. As far as we know, other animals don't kiss at all. They may throw or touch their faces together, but even those who have lips do not share saliva or purse and beat their lips together. They don't have to. Take wild boars. Males produce a pungent odor that females find most attractive. The main chemical is a pheromone called androstenone that stimulates the desire of females to mate. From a female point of view this is a good thing, since males with the most androstonene are also the most fertile. Her sense of smell is so acute, she doesn't need to get close enough to kiss the male. The same is true of many other mammals. For example, female hamsters emit a pheromone that greatly excites the males. A male black widow spider can smell pheromones produced by a female that tell him if she has recently eaten. To minimize the risk of being eaten, he will only mate with her if she is not hungry. The thing is that animals don't have to come close to each other to smell a good potential mate. On the other hand, humans have a menacing sense of smell, so we benefit from rapprochement. Smell is not the only clue we use to assess each other's fitness, but studies have shown it plays an important role in choosing a mate. A study published in 1995 showed that women, just like mice, prefer the smell of men who are genetically different from them. This makes sense, since mating with someone with different genes may produce healthy offspring. Kissing is a great way to get close enough to sniff out your partner's genes. In 2013, Velodarsky examined kissing preferences in detail. He asked several hundred people what was most important when kissing someone. How they smelled was very, and the importance of smell increased when women were most fertile. It turns out that males also produce a version of the pheromone that porcine females find attractive. It is present in male sweat, and when women are exposed to it their arousal levels rise slightly. Pheromones are a big part of how mammals chose a mate, says Velodarski, and we share some of them. In some cultures, this smelling behavior has morphed into physical lip contact. It's hard to identify when it happened, but they both serve the same purpose, says Velodarski. So if you want to find a perfect match, you can give up kissing and start smelling people instead. You will find an equally good mate, and you will not get half bacteria. premise: Why do so few tigers eat humans? When you leave Bendhabgarh National Park in central India, there's a message showing a giant, silent tiger. The message says, maybe you haven't seen me, but I've seen you. There are more than a billion people in India and Indian tigers probably see humans every day of their lives. Tigers can and do kill almost anything they meet in the jungle, they will kill even attacking elephants and rhinos. Surely, then, it is a little strange that attacks on humans are not more frequent. Some people would argue that these attacks were actually common in the past. British writers of adventure stories, such as Jim Corbett, gave the impression that village life in India in the early years of the twentieth century entailed a phase of constant siege by man-eating tigers. But perhaps they exaggerated the terror spread by tigers. There were also a lot more tigers around in those days (probably 60.000 in the subcontinent compared to only 3000 today). So proportionally, it seems that the attacks were as rare then as they are today. The prevailing assumption is that constraint is fear; but what exactly are tigers afraid of? Can they really know that maybe we are armed even better than them? Surely not. Has the species engineered the experiences of all tigers with humans whose genes would be inherited as instinct? Possibly. But I think the explanation may be simpler and, in a way, more intriguing. Since the growth of ethology in the 1950s. We were trying to understand animal behavior from the animals' point of view. Until the first elegant experiments of pioneers in the field like Conrad Lorenz, naturalists wrote about animals as if they were slightly less intelligent humans. Jim Corbett's breathless reports of his duel with the Ann Eaters actually tell us more about Jim Corbett than the animals. The principle of ethology, on the other hand, requires us to try to think in the same way as the animal we study thinks, and to observe every tiny detail of its behavior without imposing our human meaning on its actions. I suspect that tigers fearing humans lies not in pre-programmed ancestral logic but in the way it actually perceives us visually. If you think like a tiger, a person in a car may only be seen as part of the car, and since tigers don't eat cars the person is safe - unless the car is threatening the tiger or its cubs, in which case a brave or furious tiger might argue. A man on foot is a different kind of puzzle. Imagine a tiger sees a person who is 1.8 meters tall. The height of a tiger is less than 1 meter but may be up to 3 meters long from head to tail. So when a tiger sees the man in the face, it may not be unreasonable to assume that the man is 6 meters long. If he encounters a deer that size, he might attack the animal by jumping on its back, but when he looks behind the brain he can't see a back. Up front the man is huge, but looking from the side he almost disappears. It must be very worrying. A hunter needs to be sure he can handle his prey, and no one is safe when they are harassed. This is especially true of a lone hunter like the tiger and may explain why lions - especially young lionesses - who tend to encourage each other to take more dangerous risks than tigers. If the theory whereby a tiger is bothered to discover that a standing human is both very large and yet somehow invisible is true, the opposite should be true of a crouching human. A crouching individual is half its size and exhibits the double dorsal spread, and more closely resembles a medium-sized deer. If tigers were simply frightened of all humans, then a kneeling man would be no more appealing as a target than a standing one. However, this does not seem to be the case. Numerous incidents of attacks on people in which villagers kneel or bend down to cut grass for forage or hardware. The fact that humans stand upright may therefore be not only something that distinguishes them from almost all other species, but also a factor that has helped them survive in a dangerous and unpredictable environment.

premise: Why companies should welcome organisation disorder is big business. Whether it's about our lives - all those inboxes and calendars - or the way companies are built, a multibillion-dollar industry helps meet that need. We have more strategies for time management, project management and self-organization than at any other time in human history. We are told that we must organize our society, our home life, our week, our day and even our sleep, all as a means to be more productive. Every week countless seminars and workshops are held around the world to tell a paying public that they have to build their lives to achieve this. This rhetoric has also crept into the thinking of business leaders and entrepreneurs, to the delight of self-proclaimed perfectionists with the need to do everything right. THE NUMBER OF BUSINESS SCHOOLS AND GRADUATES HAS GROWN MASSIVELY OVER THE LAST 50 YEARS, AND HAS BASICALLY TAUGHT PEOPLE HOW TO ORGANIZE WELL. Ironically, however, the number of businesses that fail is steadily increasing. Work-related stress is increasing. A large proportion of workers from all demographics claim to be unhappy with the way their work is structured and the way they are managed. This begs the question: What went wrong? Why on paper does the impulse to organize seem a sure chance of increasing productivity, but in reality it is much lower than expected? This has been a problem for some time. Frederick Taylor was one of the fathers of scientific management. Writing in the first half of the 20th century, he devised a number of principles for improving the efficiency of the labor process, which have since become widespread in modern societies. So the approach has been around for a while. New research suggests that this obsession with efficiency is misguided. The problem is not necessarily the management theories or strategies we use to organize our work; it is the basic assumptions we hold in approaching the way we work. Here it is assumed that order is a necessary condition for productivity. This assumption also fostered the idea that disorder must impair organizational productivity. The result is that businesses and people invest time and money in organizing themselves for the sake of organizing, rather than actually looking at the ultimate goal and benefit of such an effort. What's more, recent studies show that order actually has diminishing returns. Order does increase productivity to some extent, but eventually the usefulness of the organization process, and the benefit it yields, are reduced to the point where every further increase in order reduces productivity. Some argue that in business, if the cost of formally building something exceeds the benefit of making it, then this thing should not be formally structured. Instead, the resources involved could be better used elsewhere. In fact, research shows that when innovating, the best approach is to create an environment free of structure and hierarchy and allow everyone involved to engage as one organic group. These environments can lead to new solutions that will never be achieved under conventional structured environments (full of bottlenecks in terms of information flow, power structures, rules and routines). In recent times companies have slowly begun to embrace this disorganization. Many of them adopt it in terms of perception (adopting the idea of disorder, as opposed to fearing it) and in terms of process (putting in place mechanisms to reduce structure). For example, Oticon, a large Danish manufacturer of hearing aids, has used what it calls a 'spaghetti' structure in order to reduce the organization's rigid hierarchies. This included abolishing official job titles and granting staff huge amounts of ownership of their time and projects. This approach proved highly successful initially, with clear improvements in employee productivity in all aspects of the business. Similarly, the former General Electric chairman embraced disorganization and raised the idea of a 'borderless organization'. Again, this involves breaking down the barriers between different parts of society and encouraging virtual collaboration and flexible working. Google and a number of other technology companies have adopted (at least in part) flexible structures of this kind, designed by technology and strong company values that stick people together. Like order, disorder should only be embraced insofar as it is beneficial. But we should not fear it - nor admire each other. This study also shows that we must continually question whether our existing assumptions work or not.

premise: Why do pagodas not fall in a country swept by typhoons and shaken by earthquakes, how did the tallest and seemingly thinnest old buildings in Japan remain 500 standing wooden pagodas for centuries? Records show only two have collapsed over the past 1400 years. Those who disappeared were destroyed by fire as a result of lightning or civil war. The devastating earthquake in Hanshin in 1995 killed 6,400 people, brought down elevated highways, flattened office blocks and devastated Cuba's port region. However it left the spectacular five-story pagoda at Toji Temple in nearby Kyoto intact, though it leveled several buildings in the neighborhood. Japanese researchers have been surprised for eons why these tall, slender buildings are so stable. Only thirty years ago the construction industry felt confident enough to erect steel and reinforced concrete office blocks that had more than a dozen floors. With its special shock absorbers to suppress the impact of sudden sideways movements from an earthquake, the thirty-six-story Kasumigaseki building in central Tokyo in Japan's first skyscraper was considered a masterpiece of modern engineering when it was built in 1968. In 826, however, with only pegs and wedges to keep his wooden structure upright, the master builder Kubudaishi did not hesitate to send his majestic Toji Pagoda soaring fifty-five feet into the sky nearly half the height of Kasumigasaki's skyscraper built some eleven centuries later. Obviously the Japanese carpenters of that time knew some tricks about allowing the building to swing and settle instead of fighting the forces of nature. But what kind of tricks? The multi-storey pagoda came to Japan from China in the 6th century. As in China, they were first introduced with Buddhism and were attached to important temples. The Chinese built their pagodas in brick or stone, with an internal staircase, and used them in later centuries primarily as watchtowers. When the pagoda arrived in Japan, however, its architecture was freely adapted to local conditions they were built less tall, usually five rather than nine stories, made mostly of wood and the staircase was discontinued because the Japanese pagoda had no practical use but became more of an art object. Because of the typhoons that hit Japan in the summer, Japanese builders learned to extend the gutters of buildings beyond the walls. This prevents rainwater from flowing down the walls. Pagodas in China and Korea have nothing like the hanging found in pagodas in Japan. The roof of a Japanese temple building can be made to hang off the walls of the structure by fifty percent or more of the total width of the building. For the same reason, the builders of Japanese pagodas seem to have further increased their weight by choosing to cover these extended eaves not with the porcelain tiles of many Chinese pagodas but with much heavier clay tiles. But this does not completely explain the great robustness of the Japanese pagodas. Is the answer that like a tall pine tree, the Japanese pagoda with its massive trunk-like central pillar known as a shinbasira simply bends and wobbles during a typhoon or earthquake? For centuries many thought so. But the answer is not so simple because the amazing thing is that the shinabashira actually does not carry any load at all. In fact, in some pagoda designs, it is not even laid on the ground, but hangs from the top of the pagoda hanging loosely in the middle of the building. The weight of the building is supported entirely by twelve external pillars and four internal pillars. And what is the role of the Shinbashira, the central pillar? The best way to understand the role of the Shinbashira is to watch a video made by Shozo Ishida, a structural engineer at the Kyoto Institute of Technology. Mr Ishida, known to his students as 'Professor Pagoda' because of his passion to understand the pagoda, built a series of models and tested them on a 'shake table' in his lab. In short, the Shinbashira acted like an enormous stationary pendulum. The ancient craftsmen, apparently without the aid of very advanced mathematics, seemed to have understood the principles applied, more than a thousand years later, in the construction of the first skyscraper in Japan. What those early craftsmen found by trial and error was that under pressure a loose pile of pagoda floors could be caused to slide back and forth independently of each other. Viewed from the side, the pagoda appears to be doing a snake dance as each successive floor moves in the opposite direction to its neighbors above and below. The Shinbashira, which ran through a hole in the center of the building, forced individual floors to move too far because after moving a certain distance they knocked in it and transferred energy along the pillar. Another curious feature of the Japanese pagoda is that because the building tapers, with each successive floor plan smaller than the one below, none of the vertical pillars bearing the weight of the building are attached to its corresponding post above. In other words, a five-story pagoda does not contain even a single pillar that runs straight through the building to carry the structural loads from top to bottom. More surprising is the fact that the personal stories of a Japanese pagoda, unlike their counterparts elsewhere, are not actually related to each other. They just pile on top of each other like a pile of hats. Interestingly, such a design would not be allowed under current Japanese building regulations. And the extra-wide eaves? Think of them as the balance pole of a rope walker. The greater the mass at each end of the rod, the easier it is for the rope procedure to maintain its equilibrium. The same is true of a pagoda. “As the eaves extend from all sides like balancing pillars,” Mr. Ishida says, “the building responds to even the strongest jolt of an earthquake with graceful oscillations, never sudden tremors.” Here again, Japanese master builders from a thousand years ago were looking forward to the concepts of modern structural engineering.
hypothesis: The builders of the pagodas knew how to absorb some of the power produced by adverse weather conditions.
label: e

premise: Why zoos are good Scientist David Hoon argues for zoos In my opinion, it is quite possible that many species of animals living in zoos or wildlife parks will have a higher or higher quality of life than in the wild. Animals in good zoos are given a varied and high-quality diet with all the necessary supplements, and any disease they have will be treated. Their movement may be somewhat restricted, but they have a safe environment to live in, and are spared bullying and social ostracism by others of their kind. They do not suffer from the threat or stress of predators, or irritation and pain from parasites or injuries. THE AVERAGE CAPTIVE ANIMAL WILL HAVE A GREATER LIFE EXPECTANCY COMPARED TO THE WILD EQUIVALENT, AND WILL NOT DIE FROM DROUGHT, STARVATION, OR IN THE JAWS OF A PREDATOR. A lot of very nasty things happen to truly 'wild' animals that just don't happen in good zoos, and to see a life that is' free 'as such that is automatically' good 'is, in my opinion, a mistake. Furthermore, zoos serve a number of key purposes. First, zoos aid conservation. A huge number of species are extinct worldwide, and many others are increasingly threatened and therefore risk extinction. Moreover, some of these collapses were sudden, dramatic and unexpected, or were simply discovered very late in the day. A species protected in captivity can be bred to provide a reservoir population against population crash or extinction in the wild. A significant number of species exist only in captivity, with many of them living in zoos. Even more only exist in the wild because they have been reintroduced from zoos, or have wild populations that have been kept by captive-bred animals. Without these efforts there would be fewer species alive today. Although reintroduction successes are few, numbers are increasing, and the very fact that species have been saved or reintroduced as a result of captive breeding proves the value of such initiatives. Zoos also provide education. Many children and adults, especially those in cities, will never see a wild animal beyond a fox or a pigeon. While it is true that television documentaries are becoming increasingly detailed and impressive, and many examples of natural history are on display in museums, there is really nothing to compare to seeing a living creature in the flesh, hearing it, smelling it, watching what it does and being able to absorb details. This alone will bring greater understanding and perspective to many, and hopefully give them a greater appreciation for wildlife, conservation efforts and how they can contribute. In addition to all this, there is also the education that can take place in zoos through signs, talks and presentations that directly convey information to visitors about the animals they see and their place in the world. It was an area where previously zoos were lacking, but now they are increasingly sophisticated in their communication and outreach work. Many zoos also work directly to educate conservation workers in other countries, or send their animal keepers abroad to contribute their knowledge and skills to those working in zoos and reserves, thus helping to improve conditions and reintroduction all over the world. Zoos also play a key role in research. If we are to save wild species and restore and repair ecosystems we need to know how key species live, function and react. Being able to conduct research on animals in zoos where there is less risk and fewer variables means that real changes in wild populations can be influenced. Enquiring, for example, about an animal's estrus cycle or its reproductive rate helps us manage wild populations. Procedures such as the capture and transfer of at-risk or dangerous individuals are reinforced by knowledge gained in zoos regarding dosages for anesthesia, and by experience in handling arid transport animals. It can make a real difference to conservation efforts and reduce human-animal conflict, and can provide a knowledge base to assist with the growing threats of habitat destruction and other problems. In conclusion, given the many ongoing global threats to the environment, it is difficult for me to view zoos as anything other than essential to the long-term survival of many species. They are essential not only in terms of protecting animals, but as a means of learning about them to assist those still in the wild, as well as educating and informing the general population about these animals and their world so they can assist or at least accept the need to be more environmentally aware. Without them, the world would be, and will increasingly become, a much poorer place.

premise: William Henry Parkin The man who invented synthetic dyes William Henry Parkin was born on March 12, 1838 in London, England. AS A CHILD, PERKINS' CURIOSITY SPARKED EARLY INTERESTS IN THE ARTS, SCIENCES, PHOTOGRAPHY, AND ENGINEERING. But it was a chance to stumble upon a mangled, yet functional, laboratory at his late grandfather's house that solidified the youngsters' enthusiasm for chemistry. As a pupil at the City of London School, Parkin immersed himself in the study of chemistry. His talent and dedication to the subject were seized upon by his tutor, Thomas Hall, who encouraged him to attend a series of lectures given by the eminent scientist Michael Faraday at the Royal Institution. These speeches aroused the even more enthusiasm of the young chemists, and he later went on to study at the Royal College of Chemistry, which he was able to enter in 1853, at the age of 15. AT THE TIME OF PERKINS' ENROLLMENT, THE ROYAL COLLEGE OF CHEMISTRY WAS HEADED BY THE RENOWNED GERMAN CHEMIST AUGUST WILHELM HOFFMANN. Perkins' scientific gifts soon caught Hoffman's attention and within two years he became Hoffman's youngest assistant. Not long after, Parkin made the scientific breakthrough that would bring him both fame and fortune. At the time, quinine was the only viable medical treatment for malaria. The drug is derived from the bark of the cinchona tree, native to South America, and in 1856 demand for the drug exceeded the available supply. Thus, when Hoffman made some passing comments about his desire for a synthetic substitute for quinine, it was no surprise that his star pupil was excited to face the challenge. During his vacation in 1856, Parkin spent his time in the laboratory on the top floor of his family home. He tried to produce quinine from aniline, a cheap and readily available coal tar waste product. However, despite his best efforts, he did not finish with quinine. Instead, it produced a mysterious dark sludge. Fortunately, Perkins's scientific and nature training prompted him to investigate the material further. While incorporating potassium dichromate and alcohol in aniline at various stages of the experimental process, he finally produced a deep purple solution. Proving the veracity of the words of the famous scientist Louis Pasteur that chance favors only the prepared mind, Parkin saw the potential of his unexpected find. Historically, textile dyes were made from natural sources such as plants and animal secretions. Some of these, like the glandular mucus of snails, were hard to come by and outrageously expensive. Indeed, the purple dye produced from a snail was once so expensive that in society at that time only the rich could afford it. Moreover, natural dyes tended to be muddy in hue and fade quickly. Against this background, the discovery of Perkins was discovered. Parkin quickly realized that his purple solution could be used to dye fabric, thus making it the world's first synthetic dye. Realizing the importance of this breakthrough, he lost no time in patenting it. BUT PERHAPS THE MOST FASCINATING RESPONSE FROM ALL PERKINS' RESPONSES TO HIS FIND WAS HIS ALMOST IMMEDIATE RECOGNITION THAT THE NEW DYE HAD COMMERCIAL POSSIBILITY.28PARKIN ORIGINALLY CALLED HIS DYE TYRIAN PURPLE, BUT LATER IT BECAME POPULARLY KNOWN AS VIOLET (FROM THE FRENCH FOR THE PLANT USED TO MAKE THE DYE PURPLE). He sought the advice of Scottish Paint Works owner Robert Polar, who assured him that the production of paint would be worth it if the paint remained fast (i.e. did not fade) and the cost was relatively low. Therefore, over the fierce objections of his teacher Hoffman, he left college to give birth to the modern chemical industry. With the help of his father and brother, Parkin set up a factory not far from London. Taking advantage of the cheap and abundant coal tar that was an almost limitless product of London gas street lighting, the paint works began producing the world's first synthetically painted material in 1857. The company received a commercial boost from Empress Eugenie of France, when she decided the new colour flattered her. Soon, purple was the necessary shade for all fashionable women in that country. In order not to faint, the Queen of England Victoria also appeared in public wearing a purple dress, thus making it a rage in England as well. The color was bold and fast, and the public demanded more. Parkin went back to the drawing board. Although Perkins fame was achieved and promised his fortune at his first discovery, the chemist continued his research. Among the other colors he developed and introduced were aniline red (1859) and aniline black (1863), and in the late 1860s, Perkins green. Importantly, Perkins's synthetic dye discoveries had results far beyond mere decorativeness. Colors have also become essential to medical research in many ways. For example, they have been used to stain bacteria and previously invisible bacteria, allowing researchers to identify in bacteria such as tuberculosis, cholera and anthrax. Artificial colors continue to play a crucial role today. And in what has been particularly pleasing to Perkin, their current use is in the search for a malaria vaccine.
