premise: Working in films When people ask French translator Virginie Verdier what she does for a living, it must be tempting to say enigmatically: Oh me? I'm in the movies. That's certainly true, but her starring role is behind the scenes. According to the translation, it doesn't become any more entertaining or glamorous than movie subtitles. If you are very lucky, you can work on the new blockbuster movies before they hit the cinema, and if you are just lucky, you can work on the blockbuster movies that go to video or DVD. The process starts when you get the original script and tape. Let's start with the translation and adaptation of the film script. The next step is what we call scheduling, that is, synchronizing the subtitles to the dialogue and images. This task requires discipline. You play the movie, listen to the voice and the subtitles appear on your screen ready for scheduling. You add your subtitle when you hear the appropriate dialogue and delete. Same at the end of the dialogue. The videotape carries a time code that operates in hours, minutes, seconds and frames. Think of it like clockwork. The subtitle unit has an insert key to capture the time code where you want the subtitle to appear. When you press the delete key, it captures the time code where you want the title to disappear. So every subtitle will be subtitled is an exact part of the translation profession. Melanie Leichon chats to Virginie Verdier of the London translation company VSI about the glamour and grind. Virginie is quick to point out that this is as accurate as any translation work. You work hard. It's not all entertainment while you're doing the translation. You need all the skills of a good translator and those of a first class editor. You have to be precise and of course much more concise than in a traditional translation job. There is an entry point and an exit point that represent the exact time at which the subtitle enters and exits. This process is then accompanied by a manual review, subtitle-by-subtitle, and adjusted timecodes to improve synchronization and respect photographic changes. This process involves playing the film literally frame by frame because it is essential that the subtitles respect the visual rhythm of the film. Different subtitles use different techniques. I'd go through the film and do all the translation and then go right back from the beginning and start the scheduling process. But you can do it in different stages, translate say 20 minutes of the movie, then schedule that segment and translate the next 20 minutes, and so on. It's just another method. For multilingual projects, scheduling is done first to create a so-called locator list, a subtitle template, which is essentially a list of English subtitles that have been pre-scheduled and edited for translation purposes. This is then translated and the timing is adjusted to the target language with the help of the translator for quality control. Like any translation job, you can't rush to write subtitles, Virginie says. If subtitles are translated and scheduled quickly, the quality will be affected and it will appear. Mistakes usually occur when the translator does not master the source language and misunderstands the original dialogue. Our work also includes reviewing and reprocessing subtitles when the translation does not meet the standard. However, the reason for redoing subtitles is not only because of poor quality translation. We may have to adapt subtitles for a new version of the film: the time code may be different. The film may have been edited or the subtitles were created for cinema rather than video. If subtitles were made for cinema in 35mm, we would have to redesign the timing for video, since subtitles could be out of sync or too fast. If the translation is good, of course we will respect the work of the original translator. On a more practical level, there are general subtitle rules to follow, Virginie says. Subtitles should appear at the bottom of the screen and usually in the center. According to her, different countries use different standards and rules. In Scandinavian countries and the Netherlands, for example, subtitles are traditionally left unjustified. Characters usually appear in white with a thin black border for easy reading on a white or light background. We can also use different colors for each speaker when subtitling for the hearing impaired. Subtitles should consist of a maximum of two lines and the maximum number of characters in each line should be between 32 and 39. Our company standard is 37 (different companies and countries have different standards). Translators often have a favorite genre, whether war films, musicals, comedies (one of the most difficult because of the subtleties and nuances of comedy in different countries), drama or corporate programs. Each requires a certain tone and style. VSI employs American subtitles, which is incredibly useful because many of the films we write are American, Virginie says. For an English person, it wouldn't be so easy to understand the meaning behind generally American phrases, and vice versa.
hypothesis: For translators, all subtitle work on films is desirable.
label: e

premise: You and your resume is the first thing a future employer sees about you, and if it's not true, may be the last. An employer will do nothing more than glance at your resume, it is estimated that most employers spend more than twenty seconds looking at each resume, so you have very little time to make an impression. Here are some tips to help you get the most out of those 20 seconds. What it should look like The first rule of all resumes is to keep them clear and simple anything complicated or lengthy tends to be rejected immediately. Achieving this is a matter of making good use of lists, bullet points and note form, and keeping your resume at the right length. There are no set rules as to how long it should be, and it will vary, of course, depending on your age, experience etc., but keep it to one page if you can that length is convenient for your reader to work with. As for the style, there are different types of layouts that you can follow refer to the examples on this site to see which one you prefer, but the basic rule is to use the headings well to clearly signal where all the relevant information is. Be sure to include the following sections: qualifications, skills, education, work experience, references, personal interests/hobbies, personality traits, then label them clearly so that your potential employer can find the information they want quickly and easily. Content resumes tend to follow a fixed order. They start with your personal details such as name, address and contact details, then move on to personal qualities such as those things in your personality that might attract an employer such as conscientious, adventurous, punctual, etc., and your career goals. After that comes the main part of your resume starting with education, then work experience. Use reverse chronological order to list these, starting with what you are doing now. The most common go back no more than ten years. Give your job details such as job titles, the names of the organizations you worked for, an outline of your job duties and then state your specific accomplishments. Then proceed to your personal interests and finish with the details of some good and reliable judges. Your future employer may not follow these, but they make an impression. Do's and don'ts A look at your resume should make a good impression. Don't make spelling mistakes, and don't send anything crumpled or with coffee stains on it. Any such thing leads to immediate rejection. Use good quality A4 paper and don't send anything but a cover letter. Diplomas, recommendations, etc., will be requested later ~ they are interested in you. When you think you're done writing your resume, read it very carefully. Check your full stops, use of bullets, indentation, use of capital letters, etc., and never include anything on your resume that is not true. It is very easy for an employer to check, and if your resume does not match what they reveal, then your chances of getting this job are probably gone. Finally, follow the instructions in the job advertisement very carefully. If they require three copies, send them three copies, not two or four. Make sure you meet the deadline too, and put the correct stamp on your envelope. You will need to accompany your resume with a cover letter. It should be adapted for each position to which you are applying. Follow the link below for tips on how to write a cover letter. And last of all good luck! Remember to Include: Career History Skills and Strengths Awards and Achievements Contact Information
hypothesis: The style of the resume varies from country to country.
label: n

premise: Temple of Zeus holds secrets of ancient game Athens has been preparing for the 2004 Summer Games. But today's games offer a far different spectacle than the competitions of ancient Greece, where naked youths with oiled bodies raced and wrestled and boxed to honor their god. These great Panhellenic events began more than 2,700 years ago, first in Olympia and later in Delphi, Lethmia and Nemea. And in Nemea, where the Games began in 573 B.C., a Berkeley archaeologist patiently restored a site whose legends helped inspire the modern Olympics. For Stephen J. Miller, exploring the site at Nemea, 70 miles from Athens, involves more than analyzing artifacts and ruins, dating ancient rock layers or patiently assembling broken pottery fragments. It also means reliving the events he learns. In the past two summers, large crowds have flocked to ancient Nemai Stadium (capacity of 40,000) to watch a modern revamp of the ancient Nemean Games. Seven hundred runners from 45 countries barefoot and dressed in white tunics scurried around the reborn stadium in groups of 12. The winners of the races were crowned just as they were in antiquity with wild celery wreaths. Miller is a professor of classics at the University of California, Berkeley, but he was also a barefoot runner, a waterbearer slave for athletes and a priest conducting the revamped ceremonies of the legendary Nemean Games. These role-playing gives you a deeper sense of antiquity and a feel for the spirit of the people who lived and worked and played there so long ago, said recently after returning from this year's fieldwork. In excavating the site every summer since 1973, Miller and his team have found and reassembled limestone pillars that once stood proudly around the Temple of Zeus. Exactly a decade after they began the excavation and east of the temple, they found the remains of a large altar to Zeus where athletes and their coaches performed sacrifices and swore for weeks just before competition. And from ancient Greek records, two years later, Millers' team also learned that his Nemea site once saw great horse races in a hippodrome that must have existed near the great stadium. At Tel Adama his team could trace faint wheel mark patterns indicating that chariots were moving there as well. In 1997 Miller and his team, looking for further evidence of a hippodrome, excavated at a spot where four low rock walls indicate that there might be a structure underneath. There they found a jug of wine, drinking mugs, coins and a crude little figure of a centaur. The next summer, after digging 20 feet, they still hadn't reached the bottom. Miller wondered what purpose might serve this deep pit with rock walls, and finally concluded that it must have been a reservoir containing large amounts of water from a river near the site that now irrigates vineyards. 'THE RESERVOIR IS A PHENOMENAL FIND, 'MILLER SAID, 'WE BELIEVE IT PROVIDED WATER FOR ABOUT 150 HORSES THAT RACED AT THE HIPPODROME DURING THE GAMES. But how did they feed the horses? And what did they do with so much junk every day? Trying to answer such questions is one of the joys of the whole project. Eight months after finding the repository, Miller and his team uncovered an ancient room used by the Nemean athletes as the apodietrium locker room where they anointed themselves with olive oil. They would then walk 120 feet through an entrance tunnel vaulted by the Asdos crypt whose walls are still marked with graffiti scratched by the athletes on their way to the stadium. The wine jug and glasses uncovered in one layer of the buried reservoir may have been left by victors in one of the ancient Nemean races, but what type of wine they drank remains unknown. Today, the local red wine served in monastic taverns is called Blood of Hercules, honoring the hero who strangled the ferocious Nemean lion there more than 5,000 years ago. AS WITH SO MUCH ARCHAEOLOGY, THE DISCOVERIES MILLER MADE IN NAMIA SEEM TO RECALL ANCIENT LEGENDS AND LINK THEM TO REALITY. The Berkeley team, for example, unveiled a tiny bronze figurine identified as the likeness of a baby named Opelts, whose fate inspired the first Nemesis Games. As Miller tells the story, Opelts was the son of Lycurgus and Eurydick, who had been trying for many years to produce an heir. When the oracle at Delphi warned them that their child should not touch the ground until he learned to walk, they ordered a female slave to take care of the infant day and night. One day, as seven warrior heroes passed through Nemea on their way to march against the fortress of Thebes they were the legendary Seven Against Thebes whose bloody war was commemorated by Aeschylus the nurse placed the child on a bed of wild celery while she offered drinks to the heroes. Immediately a snake lurking in the vegetation killed the infant and the warriors re-named the boy Archmorus, Begins of Doom, and held the first Nemean Games in his honor as a funeral festival. Bouquets of wild celery crowned the winners of these Games, as they did the modern-day winners at Nemea last summer. As with all classical archaeologists, whose excavations shed so startling light on antiquity, Miller and his students are now ready to organize and classify their prized finds from the summer season, and plan to excavate in the seasons to come. 'In the mound of earth where we saw the imprints of wheel cuts, we also have a bronze vessel of the kind that was always used to pour libations, 'Miller said. This mound goes back to 600 BC, so now we wonder what happened there in that religious and athletic complex even before the Nemean Games. Archaeology isn't cheap, and each season in Nemea costs at least $150,000 for the staff, equipment and 35 local workers from the nearby town of modern-day Nemea, which Miller calls the core of the project. All the money comes from private sources and nothing less than Millers jobs are lecturing to the public and scouring the grounds for donations.
hypothesis: Religion played a key role in the games.
label: e

premise: Plans for zoo conservation One of London zoos recent adverts caused me some irritation, so it clearly distorted reality. Entitled No Zoos Can These Animals Be Told to Fill Up, it bordered on illustrations of some endangered species and went on to conjure up the myth that without zoos like London Zoo these animals would almost certainly disappear forever. With a fairly mediocre record of the zoo worlds on conservation, one could be forgiven for being a little skeptical about such an advertisement. Zoos were originally conceived as places of recreation, and their proposed involvement in conservation did not arise in earnest until about 30 years ago, when the Zoological Society of London held the first official international meeting on the subject. Eight years later, a series of global conferences were held, entitled Growing Endangered Species, and from that point on conservation became the watchword of the zoo community. This commitment has now been clearly defined in the Global Zpo Conservation Strategy (WZGS, September 1993), which although an important and welcome document is indeed based on unrealistic optimism about the nature of the zoo industry. The WZCS estimates that there are about 10,000 zoos in the world, of which about 1,000 represent a core of quality collections capable of participating in coordinated conservation programs. It's probably the papers that first failed, as I believe 10,000 is a serious underestimate of the total number of places masquerading as zoological factories. Of course, accurate figures are hard to come by, but to put the issue in perspective, I found that in a year of work in Eastern Europe I discover fresh zoos almost on a weekly basis. The second flaw in the reasoning of the WZCS document is the naive faith it places in its 1,000 core zoos. One might assume that the caliber of these institutions would have been carefully examined, but it seems that the criterion for inclusion in this select list may simply be that the zoo is a member of a federation or zoo association. This may be a good starting point, working on the assumption that members must meet certain standards, but again the facts do not support the theory. The highly respected American Association of Zoological Parks and Aquariums (AAZPA) had highly dubious members, and in Britain the Federation of Zoological Gardens of Great Britain and Ireland has occasionally 24Reading had members who were categorically censored in the national press. These include the Robin Hill Adventure Park on the Isle of Wight, which many have seen for the country's most notorious animal collection. This institution, which for years had been protected by the islands' local council (who considered it a tourist convenience), was finally closed following a damning report from a veterinary inspector appointed under the terms of the Zoo Licensing Act 1981. Since there has always been a collection of dubious reputations, it is imperative to think about the standards that the Zoo Federation sets when granting membership. The situation is even worse in developing countries where little money is available for redevelopment and it is difficult to see a way to integrate collections into the overall scheme of the WZCS. Even assuming that the core zoos of the 1,000 WZCSs are all of a high standard with scientific staff and research facilities, trained and dedicated keepers, accommodation that allows normal or natural behaviour and a policy of fully cooperating with each other what could be the potential for conservation? Colin Tudegg, author of The Last Animals in the Zoo (Oxford University Press, 1992), argues that if the world's zoos worked together in cooperative breeding programs, then even without further expansion they could save about 2,000 species of endangered terrestrial vertebrates. This seems an extremely optimistic proposition from a man who must be aware of the failings and weaknesses of the zoo industry, the man who, when he was a member of the London Zoo Council, had to persuade the zoo to devote more of its activities to conservation. Moreover, where are the facts supporting such optimism? Today it can be said that about 16 species have been saved by captive breeding programs, although the number of such can hardly be seen as resounding successes. Beyond that, about 20 more species are being seriously considered for the zoo's conservation plans. Given that the international conference at London Zoo took place 30 years ago, that's pretty slow progress, and a far cry from Todgs' target of 2,000.
hypothesis: The number of successful zoo conservation programs is not satisfying.

Cancer Research UK said yesterday that it was excited by the potential of Prof Seymour's pioneering techniques. Cancer-killing viruses take advantage of the fact that cancer cells suppress the body's local immune system.\ If cancer doesn't, the immune system wipes it out. If you can get a virus into a tumor, viruses find them a very good place to be because there is no immune system to prevent them from replicating. You can treat this as the Achilles heel of cancer.\ Only a small amount of the virus should reach the cancer. “They replicate, get a million copies in each cell and the cell bursts and they infect the nearby tumour cells and repeat the process,” Prof Seymour said. After the stealth virus infects the tumor, it replicates, but the copies have no chemical changes. For safety reasons, both have been disabled to make them less pathogenic in the trial, but Prof Seymour said he hoped to eventually use natural viruses.
